subsubtopic: CALL FOR CENSURE OF HON. MEMBER FOR VAUDREUIL- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The Liberal member of Parliament for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) has widely circulated a copy of his letter to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) dated November 17 in which he stated:
It is reported that you are prepared to concede even more power to Prince Edward Island. This island has a population about equal to that in my constituency yet it has four MPs and a complete provincial government with powers that exceed those of the government of the state of California.
There has to be a limit. Prince Edward Island is too small a tail wagging too big a dog.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley):
That this House censures the member of Parliament for Vaudreuil for promoting national disunity by his vicious attack on Prince Edward Island, the cradle of confederation, and for his most hateful campaign to deny the province of Prince Edward Island a genuine role in future constitutional decisions.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) is on record as saying that acid rain is costing the Canadian taxpayer and the Canadian environment hundreds of millions of dollars per year in damage, in view of the same minister's statement that at least $400 million must be spent to deal with the problem of acid rain and that that money has not been allocated, and in view of the fact that the Liberal government is not acting in the best interests of Canadians by reducing the amount of acid rain through budgetary measures and policy, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae):
That this House unanimously call for producer-pay legislation so that the producers of acid rain, in both Canada and the United States, may be presented with bills on a quarterly basis for the damage and destruction they now cause to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday in an interview with the Montreal Gazette and as published this morning in the Montreal Gazette-I am sure that the minister or at least his staff would have noticed the article-the Minister of Finance indicated that Canadians would have to get used to a lower standard of living in order to combat energy prices. These comments are consistent with comments made by officials of the minister's department last week, that as far as they were concerned Canadians will also have to endure lower real wages in order to combat inflation.
Would the minister tell the House whether or not that is the policy of this government and, if so, how long will Canadians have to endure a lower standard of living in order to put up with the government's failure to come forward with an energy policy which would assist Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is referring to an interview I had yesterday on a very complex subject. I am not in any way disowning any of the comments I made in that interview, which were a series of economic observations including the fact that all industrialized countries, including Canada, are facing lower growth rates and that it is unlikely that in the immediate future any industrialized country will achieve the growth rate which was part of our public consciousness in the past decade. That is what I said and I believe that is the case.
I also believe it is essential to understand at the present time what is required in the way of economic behaviour if we wish to make any impact on the very troublesome question of inflation.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the same article it is reported as follows: "MacEachen mused, noting the tendency is to blame inflation always on someone else". The minister then went on to explain that inflation should be placed at the door of individuals, of enterprise of union economic decisions

November 21, 1980
Oral Questions
and a host of other areas, and not once, according to the Gazette portion of the report, does he mention the government might have something to do with the high rate of inflation.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: They are the real culprits.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Given the minister's own budget, particularly what is stated within at page 33, and the effect of that budget on low and moderate income people, at a time when the minister himself is saying that we will have to get used to lower standards of income, will the minister please review those aspects of his budget which will fall most heavily on lower and moderate income people in this country, particularly in light of the forecasts with respect to lower economic activity, lower wages and lower standards of living?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has drawn attention to the fact that no mention is made of the government's role in combating inflation.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Causing it.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I agree with him that the government does have an important role to play, and I have in the course of the budget and the policies flowing therefrom undertaken to follow certain policies which I hope will have a direct impact on the inflationary situation, not only in the field of fiscal and monetary policy, but also in the very important area of having taken steps to improve the productivity of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the minister will understand when 1 say most Canadians believe that, as soon as the minister and his government are willing to accept responsibility for inflation, the first step will have been taken to solve part of the problem.

Let me ask a final question which relates to the minister's budget and the effect of his statement yesterday. In his budget the minister indicated he was interested in achieving significant savings in the social policy field. Indeed, his budget indicates that social policy spending will receive less and less of the government's expenditures over the next three years. 1 ask the minister to give this House an undertaking that in the government's dealings with the provinces the minister will resist any suggestion that the federal government diminish its contribution and support for the Canada Assistance Plan, which carries most of our social services in this country, and for medicare. Will the minister resist the federal government's diminishing its contribution to those two programs?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ANTI-INFLATION POLICY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have indicated in the budget and subsequently that we intended to negotiate the question of fiscal transfers to the provinces as agreements expire, and that it would be an objective of those negotiations to attempt to secure savings in that area, as in other areas of government expenditure. We have not prejudged the question,
but it will be the objective to secure savings in the general field of transfers.
The hon. member has referred specifically to the Canada Assistance Plan and to the medicare act. I assure him, as the minister in a former responsibility who piloted both these measures through the House of Commons, that I will be very respectful in any negotiation of the important role these programs play in the social security system of Canada.

Madam Speaker, 1 have a question for the Minister of Labour who does not appear to be in the House. Perhaps his parliamentary secretary can answer the question.
Does the Department of Labour agree with this new policy of the Minister of Finance that Canadian workers should be required to bear the brunt of the anti-inflation fight by requiring them to accept lower real wages? If so, could the Minister of Labour explain to this House why that draconian measure should be borne by the workers of this country and almost exclusively, in the minister's view, by them?

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND HYDROELECTRICITY EXPORTS-CORRIDOR THROUGH QUEBEC-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Today in the Newfoundland legislature the government of Newfoundland announced it was taking away the water rights of the Churchill Falls Power Corporation. They did that out of a sense of complete exasperation and frustration over their inability to reach an agreement with Quebec. The minister knows the consequences of that.
I therefore ask this question. A few days ago the Economic Council of Canada released the results of a special study it conducted on the Newfoundland economy. One of their findings was that the Newfoundland economy was losing annually $600 million a year to Quebec in shortfall as a result of that iniquitous power contract. In light of the findings of the Economic Council of Canada and the importance it places on the development of hydro, and in view of the move in St. John's today by the Newfoundland government, I ask the minister quite earnestly if he will now exercise the constitutional authority he has under section 92(10) and grant the request of the government of Newfoundland to provide a corridor through Quebec so that Newfoundland can develop its power and sell it on the open market?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND HYDROELECTRICITY EXPORTS-CORRIDOR THROUGH QUEBEC-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member refers to a study which has been published. He knows that this study has already been challenged in various quarters as to a certain number of its assumptions. I am in no position to pass honest judgment on that particular study, and I will let the matter stand where it is now.
As to the legislation introduced today in the Newfoundland legislature, I understand that the premier has indicated that he wants this legislation passed and referred to the courts to have the matter investigated by the courts in order to determine whether the Newfoundland legislature has authority to pass this legislation.
As to the specific point raised by the hon. member about a corridor, the Prime Minister indicated at the last federal-provincial conference of first ministers that in his view the federal government had such a right, that the federal government was

November 21, 1980
Oral Questions
prepared to exercise the rights necessary but that obviously the best solution was still a negotiated settlement.
Moreover, I remind the hon. member that any such decision by itself would have no impact on the existing contract with Churchill Falls, which obviously is a different situation where there is a contract between Hydro-Quebec and the Churchill Falls Corporation. Even if we were to agree completely with the question raised by the hon. member, it would not change the other contract, which is the point at issue at the present time. However, at the last premiers' conference the Prime Minister indicated quite clearly the point of view of the federal government in this respect.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND HYDROELECTRICITY EXPORTS-CORRIDOR THROUGH QUEBEC-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister knows that there is a direct linkage, particularly in light of the action announced today by the Newfoundland government. I believe the minister will find that there is a much greater disposition now on the part of the government of Quebec to sit down and discuss this matter rationally with the Government of Canada.
About two months ago the Premier of Newfoundland wrote to the Prime Minister of Canada telling the Prime Minister that he had a letter of intent from the power authority of the state of New York to buy power from the undeveloped Lower Churchill. That seems to fulfil the requirement which the Prime Minister laid down. To the best of my knowledge that letter has not been answered.
Will the minister now tell the House and the country that he is prepared to exercise the constitutional authority he has under the BN A Act, section 92(10), give Newfoundland what is its just requirement under the constitution and announce that a corridor through Quebec will be provided? The least he could tell us today is that he is prepared to take this matter up on an urgent basis with the government of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND HYDROELECTRICITY EXPORTS-CORRIDOR THROUGH QUEBEC-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 refer the hon. member to the very clear statement made by the Prime Minister during the constitutional conference on this very subject. The statement by the Prime Minister was unequivocal and quite clear.
As to the question of dealing with the government of Quebec and the government of Newfoundland, I can tell the hon. member that I have had discussions with the minister of energy of Newfoundland and indicated that we would stand ready to sit down with the government of Newfoundland and the government of Quebec to try to iron out these particular issues which are outstanding. Until now I have not been able to get a positive answer from the government of Newfoundland that it is willing to participate in such discussions. 1 indicated that if the government of Quebec and the government of Newfoundland were willing to have the federal government sit down with them and try to work out in an amicable way a resolution of these very difficult questions, we would stand ready to help and try to work things out. I must say that I have not been able to get a positive response as yet from the government of Newfoundland to this particular offer.
1 have made the same offer to the government of Quebec, that we are standing ready to help if the government of Quebec felt
we could contribute anything in terms of resolving this difficult situation in an amicable way.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND HYDROELECTRICITY EXPORTS-CORRIDOR THROUGH QUEBEC-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is a very important matter, and 1 am sure you appreciate that. subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND HYDROELECTRICITY EXPORTS-CORRIDOR THROUGH QUEBEC-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I suggest the type of false rhetoric such as that used by the hon. member does not help resolve this kind of issue. We have never indicated that we were applying a double standard or that we were refusing to exercise our constitutional jurisdiction. We have indicated that we are going to apply the same standard and exactly the same regime, but the fact is that in this particular instance it would be much better and easier for all concerned, including the government of Newfoundland, if this question could be resolved in a negotiated way rather than by using rhetoric and the kind of abusive language the hon. member is using.
I submit to the hon. member that there are better ways of doing things. In the case of electricity, for instance, there might be the economic necessity and it might be much more advisable to wheel power through the Quebec hydro system. In the case of pipelines we do not have to go through provincial pipelines to carry oil or gas. In the case of electricity it becomes economically much more advisable and feasible to use the existing systems.
However, we have indicated that we stand ready to exercise our constitutional power, and I want to make it quite clear that there are no double standards for this government. There are not two constitutions in this country; there is one constitution, and we will apply it.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have received requests from some hon. members of the House to explain why I am wearing this button. There are three good reasons. The first reason is because of the pressure faced by my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). The second reason is because approximately 25 years ago two great Canadians, Mayor Vic Copps and Mayor Gaston Hardy, twinned the cities of Hamilton and Shawinigan. The third reason is that because I am the Minister of State for Social Development I have to be concerned for the underdog, so I am concerned about the poor, the widowed, orphans, Liberals in Alberta, and the Hamilton Tiger Cats!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question of privilege with respect to the very uncalled for and, if I may say so, snide remarks of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) with respect to a vague accusation that some members in the Conservative party interjected during one of his answers in the question period. The minister expressed the hope that it would not find its way into Hansard. I sit much closer than the minister to members on this side, and I heard no such interjection coming from a Conservative member.
I believe it does nothing for the spirit of this place when the minister makes comments such as he did which reflect on every individual member of the Conservative party, and which reflect on the very principle which he so loosely espoused while he was replying to the question, that one is presumed innocent until proven guilty. Unless the minister can point to a member of the Conservative party and attribute that interjection to
that hon. member, then I think as a gentleman and a member of this House he should withdraw any reference he made to members of this party.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: This certainly is not a question of privilege. However, the point has been made.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Allow the minister to speak.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: The people who record the proceedings of this House write down everything they hear. I am sure that they are not influenced by whatever directives or instructions they may receive from both sides.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: That is not the point.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: That is not the point. The remarks which the minister made today are on the record. I think he is rising right now to withdraw those remarks, and I would urge the Chair to allow him to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member says that what I heard, and what I suspect he heard, did not come from a member of the Conservative party. I am ready to take his word that perhaps it did not come from a member of the Conservative party. However, I think he will recognize that there was certainly a very uncalled for comment which came from somebody in the opposition benches.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Smear everybody.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is no point in making the matter worse. In the first instance the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) attributed a remark to some Conservative member. Now he says that it was someone on the opposition side, which would include my party. I heard no remark. I have asked my colleagues, and they tell me that none of them made any spurious remark. I believe that the minister should either withdraw the remark or tell us what was said and who made the comment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: I think we will all be better off when we read Hansard tomorrow.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what we have here is a statement made by a minister of the Crown which cast direct aspersions upon every member of the opposition. The minister has narrowed his statement to say that it was not a member of the Progressive Conservative Party, although he did so in a most grudging fashion. He has allowed his accusation to stand as it relates to members of the New Democratic Party.
There is now a clear breach of the privileges of every member of the New Democratic Party, but prior to that of every member of the opposition. I believe that we should not wait for Hansard but, rather, have the matter resolved now by
November 21, 1980

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD

That is not the point, because the remark is not there. I submit that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and now the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), should withdraw the charge unreservedly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Name the member or withdraw.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I heard what was stated by the Minister of the Environment very clearly. 1 heard every word of what was said and it came from the opposition benches. I have checked further with several members on this side, all of whom have confirmed that this was the case. 1 hope the hon. member who made the comment will have the courage to stand up and say so.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the two ministers are now making this problem far worse than it was at the beginning. The Minister of Energy could have solved the problem by doing the gentlemanly thing and withdrawing his accusation, but now he and his colleague are saying that they heard a remark. I have checked with the members of my party, and there was no such remark from these benches. I heard the hon.
Privilege-Mr. Nielsen
member for Winnipeg North Centre say that he has checked with all his members and that no such remark came from the NDP benches.
Why does the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources not respect the tradition of this House and withdraw, as most gentleman who sit in this place should, because the charge made by the minister is tied to the loose use of the expression "one is presumed innocent until proven guilty", leaving the inference that we do not respect that basic, fundamental tenet of the law.
If the minister would like this matter to carry on, then he will have his way, but if he wishes to do the right thing and act like a gentleman, as hon. members usually do in this House, he should withdraw his remarks without any reservation whatsoever. Such an act on the part of the minister might do something to restore some sense of co-operation and an atmosphere wherein the government's business may move along in a little more tenable way.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-STATEMENT MADE BY MR. LALONDE DURING QUESTION PERIOD

Madam Speaker, my point of order arises out of an answer given by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) today. It concerns the Canadian Transport Commission issuing a permit to the city of Winnipeg to build the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. 1 was informed this week that a permit would be issued, that it had been cleared through the Department of Justice. As I understood the minister's answer today, he said that he was going to check to see whether it was all right for the CTC to issue the permit to the city of Winnipeg.
I do not believe the minister has the authority to overrule the Canadian Transport Commission on a decision to issue a permit. 1 believe that this matter should be cleared up in the House. Did the minister mean that he was going to take this matter up with the cabinet and have the cabinet overrule the Canadian Transport Commission? Is the minister going to interfere directly with the Canadian Transport Commission to have this permit stopped? The minister does not have the authority, and I believe he should clear up this point.

THE LATE P. B. RYNARD TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with deep regret that I rise to advise this House that Dr. P. B. Rynard, member of Parliament for Simcoe North for 22 years, passed away last evening. Doctor Rynard was a great humanitarian. He was a kind and thoughtful physician. He was a well-loved representative of his constituents and a respected member of this House. He set an example for every Canadian to follow, especially those from rural and semi-rural constituencies.
We are all saddened by his death, but we acknowledge with thanks that he left Canada and Canadians better as a result of his contribution.

subtopic: THE LATE P. B. RYNARD TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE LATE P. B. RYNARD TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to express my own sorrow at the knowledge which the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) has conveyed to us about the death of a former colleague in the House of Commons.
Like many other members, I knew Dr. Rynard personally. I had extremely good personal relations with him. I benefited from his administrations from time to time, and I had the highest regard for him. He was a strong advocate of his own positions in the House of Commons. He participated actively in the question period, and at the same time he maintained a courteous attitude toward all members of the House, which I think all of us could emulate from time to time.

subtopic: THE LATE P. B. RYNARD TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada

Like other members, I benefited from his presence in the House and, like others, I will miss him very much.

At the request of the governments of Newfoundland and Labrador and Quebec, the Canadian Saltfish Corporation has, over the years, marketed frozen salmon, frozen char, cured herring and cured mackerel. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it from the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that if there has been an alteration in the motion, it was so that it would conform with the provisions of the act. This is the kind of advice which is normally given to members when they want to bring in a motion. The Table is here to assist members to do what they want in the manner in which it should be done. In my view, and I say this with reservation, that is normal practice. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is giving me notice that he will raise a question of privilege at another time. I presume he wants the debate to proceed as previously announced. I will recognize the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell).

Madam Speaker, today we begin a very unique debate. On budget night, October 28, the Liberal government announced it intended to invoke Division II of the Petroleum Administration Act of 1978. It proclaimed two regulations, one covering oil prices and the other covering gas prices.
This Division II of the Petroleum Administration Act is a drastic piece of law because it gives the federal government the power to set oil and gas prices unilaterally without the consent of the producing provinces. Once the government triggers this part of the Petroleum Administration Act and takes this power, it must within 15 days table its proclamation in the House of Commons. This was done on November 12. At that point, any ten members may pray that the proclamation be revoked. This is what I and nine other NDP members have done. 1 happen to have faster running shoes, so my motion is being debated first.
The unusual procedure may indicate that it was hoped by Parliament when it passed the Petroleum Administration Act that Division 11 might never be invoked, because there are very few parliamentary procedures like this one. As I said, it is a fairly unique procedure. Another rare example is the legislation that covered wage and price controls.
Make no mistake about it. The invoking of this Petroleum Administration Act provision is equivalent to invoking the War Measures Act in the escalating dispute with oil and gas producing provinces, especially with the province of Alberta.
Never before, short of a wartime emergency, has such a drastic power been used. In the past we settled oil and gas pricing disputes by agreement-and 1 stress by agreement- between Ottawa and the producing provinces. Indeed the constitutionality of the Petroleum Administration Act, if it is indeed constitutional, has never been tested. It appears to be grounded in the federal power over interprovincial trade supplemented, perhaps, by the emergency powers available to the federal government in section 91 of the British North America Act.
Let me make clear at the outset the position of the New Democratic Party. In principle we are not against the existence of such emergency powers, but we say that they should only be
invoked when all else has failed, and that is not the case now. There is still room for negotiation, compromise, and agreement. There is not yet a state of war between the federal government and the producing provinces, so we think it is unwise, unnecessary and dangerous to invoke the act now. I challenge the minister who is sitting across from me to explain why it was necessary for him to act so unilaterally in this matter.
I look across the floor at this Liberal government, and I despair. It is out of touch with provincial aspirations, especially those aspirations-and I use my words carefully-of Canadians who live in western Canada. This is best illustrated by the actions of the leader of hon. members opposite in his flight from responsibility to Arabia.
I do not agree with the Alberta position and that of Premier Lougheed, but I can sympathize with the frustrations of people in the west when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does not talk to his fellow Canadians in Edmonton but dances "sheik to sheik", as an hon. member said yesterday, in Saudi Arabia, as he once did in New York. The timing for that trip, in my submission, is disastrous. The symbolism is wrong. The disdain for the producing provinces of Canada is evident, outrageous, and offensive.
For his part, Premier Lougheed has invoked his own Bill 50 to cut back the supply of oil or to turn down the tap. In my view this too is an irresponsible escalation of the conflict. In Alberta they are playing with matches these days, and both the Alberta economy and the Canadian people could get burned.
I was also shocked at the support given to Premier Lough-eed's action of turning down the tap by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the Conservative financial critic, and the Conservative party to my right on the night Premier Lougheed gave his statement. 1 refer to the statements made by the hon. member for St. John's West at the press conference shortly thereafter.
I will go further and say that the Leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Clark), who should know better, is aiding and abetting the new forces of separatism in western Canada.
That is rubbish.
1 heard the hon. member say "rubbish". The party to my right is aiding and abetting separatism in western Canada.
That is rubbish.

The hon. member to my right is objecting. Why does he not stand up in the House and object? Why does he not go out to western Canada and say that? Why does his leader not stand up and say that he is totally against this?
He has.

If he takes this position, I ask hon. members to my right who are aiding and abetting separatism why their
November 21, 1980

leader has not stood up and repudiated certain reported remarks.
He has.

If the hon. member will give me a chance, let me ask why the former prime minister, who is the leader of the Conservative party, has not stood up and repudiated the remarks-or denied them-which are reported in the Vancouver Sun of Saturday, October 25. The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) was reported to have said, and I quote:
I think (Western Canada) should separate if there's no other way of resolving the situation. If we are going to keep Canada together, the four western provinces ... should speak as one.
Then the hon. member advocated a western parliament. What is a western parliament?
This is the Parliament of Canada. Such remarks aid and abet the forces of separatism in western Canada, and that has never been denied. I invite the former Prime Minister to rise on a question of privilege tomorrow and deny this statement.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He will do it tomorrow.
Let him do it tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Tomorrow is Saturday.

Let him do it on Monday.
Lest I be accused of letting hon. members opposite off lightly, let me say that we saw earlier this year a government willing to negotiate and undertake the co-operation and restraint necessary to keep our country together. I speak about its efforts in Quebec. If the Liberals would spend half the amount of effort in negotiations with the producing provinces they spent in trying to woo Quebec, I think the situation would be different. Instead, it seems to me-I say this earnestly, and I hope I am wrong-they are pushing for a fight. There is what Richard Gwyn described in his book as the Prime Minister's white anger and his determination to put his opponent down at all costs and never give up. The Arab junket has just topped this off. The people of the west now fundamentally distrust the Prime Minister, and 1 call upon the Prime Minister either to resign for the good of the country soon or to come to western Canada and be prepared to speak to and with, and not lecture or hector, Canadians who are living in the west.
Instead of a falcon for Sheik Yamani what we need is a dove from the Prime Minister to the Canadians in western Canada. The alternative is a prolongation of this family fight, and no one wins a family fight.
This is not the way we used to do things in Canada. We Canadians have prided ourselves on our ability to compromise, to reason, and to look at the greater interests of our country. Compromise and co-operation have been the Canadian tradition. What we have been seeing in the last year is not the Canadian tradition. I feel that in invoking the Petroleum Administration Act this present government is departing not
Petroleum Administration Act
only from the Canadian tradition but also from its own traditions and policies.
The late Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson developed a policy called co-operative federalism. I would like to take a moment today to talk about co-operative federalism, and to emphasize how relevant it is these days, as it was relevant to the problems of the sixties. The spirit of compromise on which it was based was very much a reflection of Mr. Pearson's own style. As a good diplomat he recognized that issues were not just black or white and that his party did not have a monopoly on wisdom. Somebody should tell the present Prime Minister that humility and tolerance of people's weaknesses can be a source of inner strength.
In this spirit, in the throne speech debate of February, 1964, then Prime Minister Pearson stressed that only through constant co-operation and consultation could the new rising demands of Quebec be resolved. I want to quote, especially for hon. members opposite, what Mr. Pearson said at that time. As reported in Hansard for February 20, 1964, at page 64 he said this:
The solution, on the essential foundation which I have mentioned, to our problems must be found in what we call co-operative federalism. That means to me that the federal government must of course always seek the approval of provincial governments, when that is necessary under our constitution, before decisions are made. That is obvious. But there must also be consultation on matters which, while within the jurisdiction of the federal government, are shared constitutionally with provincial governments, or are of such great and immediate importance to provincial governments that, for good results, provincial support and co-operation must be obtained.
Later in that speech he said, and I quote from page 65:
The issue is not, and must not, become "provincial rights" versus "Canada first". These slogans and any others which represent competing approaches to national unity are dangerous and could be destroying; and they misrepresent the actual position.
Of all the critical issues that were resolved through the spirit of co-operative federalism none was more important than the pension plan dispute of 1964. With strong opposition from Quebec and the crisis of confederation reaching a peak in those days, Pearson attempted to begin the healing process with a major speech on April 14 during the budget debate. In that speech he attempted to convince both English and French Canadians that only through compromise could conflicting goals be harmonized and the unity of the country preserved.
I should like to quote from that speech as reported in Hansard of April 14, 1964, at page 2142. It reads in part:
I refer to a problem which is very much in our minds and indeed in our hearts: the problem of Canadian unity; the problem of unity in a federation; the problem of federalism, which is basic to our growth, basic to our strength; basic to our very survival.
Politically that problem, as in every federal state, is the necessity for having a central government strong enough in jurisdiction, in resources and in resolve to discharge its responsibilities to all the people, but a central government which will not encroach on the jurisdiction of the provinces or which acts so as to prejudice their ability to do their job within their jurisdiction. The reconciliation of these two things is not easy.

-there must be co-operation for progress in order to avoid a conflict that would destroy us.-
-without this co-operation and understanding, in the face of new pressures, tensions and problems arising out of growth and change and the quiet revolutions, the nation that our forefathers founded and built, might disintegrate and disappear. We must do nothing, either by provocation or by weakness or by stubborn unawareness of the basic nature of our federalism or by words or actions based on prejudice or fear, to bring about that weakening or disappearance.
Compare these words with the Prime Minister showing up in Winnipeg-
Regina.
-showing up in Regina and telling Canadians living in western Canada that they were hysterical.
Nobody is hysterical in Winnipeg.

Finally, Mr. Pearson concluded with the following words:
It is the task of parliament, without regard to party; it is the challenge of statesmanship rising above faction, to find the solutions to our problems which are now more serious and more difficult than any we have faced in peacetime since 1867. We must find these solutions by agreement, not force them by compulsion. We cannot hope to find such agreement in our country if we cannot find a basis for it in our Parliament.
We have a lot to learn from these words. We now have a not so quiet revolution in western Canada. The west is booming economically and, strangely, while becoming wealthier, the west is becoming angry.
Pearson also once said:
We must bring about a co-operative federalism, that is to say, a federalism free from any spirit of unacceptable centralization.
Unacceptable centralization, power for the sake of power, that is what scares the west right now. A good example of this is in the budget and in the energy policy, and that is the proposed western development fund, a $4 billion fund taken from western resources to be managed by Ottawa's bureaucrats, for western Canadians. That is not co-operative federalism at all.
Members opposite should realize that the new west is proud. I have already mentioned the Prime Minister's speech in Regina. That is not co-operative federalism. Members opposite should realize that the west is not monolithic. There is not only Premier Lougheed in Alberta, there is also Grant Notley. He has been saying some things in a reasonable way. I say this to my friend, there are voices in western Canada other than the voices over here to my right of members who are apologists for the multinational oil companies.
Not all westerners are as negative as Premier Bill Bennett of British Columbia. David Barrett, the next premier of British Columbia, I hope, has advocated public ownership of the oil companies, and he carries on in what I think is the older B.C. tradition that the younger Bennett's father knew but the younger Bennett has forgotten. When Dave Barrett speaks he speaks about Canadians who live in British Columbia, but the emphasis is on Canadians first.
I did a survey in my riding, as many hon. members have done, which I sent out in my householder. I received a number of replies. It is interesting to see-and I have checked this with some of the members from Ontario-that a lot of things are very similar. The constitution is not a big issue. The bread and butter issues, such as the budget, the energy policy and so on, are the more popular issues. Here is one letter which says:
I resent being called westerners. Who are Canadians then, only Ontario? I do not mind paying more to help. I resent it all being spent in the east.
There is a feeling of partnership, a feeling of concern amongst the ordinary people, not the fascist oil company types who are heading and funding the separatist movement in Alberta right now, but among the real, ordinary people. There is a concern there that they be Canadians first. I want to stand up as a member from British Columbia, with members from the west around me, and say strongly that we are totally against any talk or movement for separatism in Canada.
Hear, hear!

However, I want to say also that this will not stop us from standing up at every opportunity-as hon. members will learn after lunch-and defending the interests of our provinces, our regions, and of Canadians living in the west.
The invocation of the Petroleum Administration Act and the slide into a real fight with Alberta, it seems to me, is also inconsistent with the Prime Minister's own writings. The Prime Minister wrote in his better days, in 1964, the following words. He wrote this in a tract called "Federalism, Nationalism, Reason", 1964, in "Future of Canadian Federalism":
Federalism is by its very essence a compromise and a pact. It is a compromise in a sense that when national consensus on all things is not desirable or cannot readily obtain, the area of consensus is reduced in order that consensus on some things be reached. It is a pact or quasi-treaty, in the sense of the terms of that compromise cannot be changed unilaterally. That is not to say that the terms are fixed forever; but only that in changing them, every effort must be made not to destroy the consensus on which the federated nation rests.
Those words were echoed in the "Canadian Forum" in 1964 by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). Therefore, the principles are there. We must return, in my view, to the spirit of co-operative federalism in this country, and that means three things. First, it means that officials from Ottawa and Alberta must meet. Not only must they meet, Mr. Speaker-and I say this to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-but they must meet, in professor Donald Smiley's words of Queen's University-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: York University.

-when he talks about co-operative federalism being a high degree of pragmatism, knowing that there cannot be any assumptions by federal officials that decisions by the central government are somehow inherently better or more legitimate than those of the provinces. I feel that the officials in the minister's department and officials in Alberta should, for the good of Canada, be more objective and work in the way described by professor Smiley.

Second, the Prime Minister must turn his JetStar around and park it on the tarmac of Edmonton airport, Regina airport or Vancouver airport, preferably on all three, and he must stay there until he has an understanding with the western governments. He must come back from Arabia.
Third, the Leader of the Opposition must rise above expedience and stop fanning the fires of separatism. He must make a strong statement in the House against it.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue my speech on the revocation of the Petroleum Administration Act proclamation. I have talked about Canadian co-operative federalism, and now I want to turn to a matter which happened the other day in the House. I asked the Prime Minister a question on the day after the announcement by Premier Lougheed of his intention to cut back oil supplies. As some members might have noticed, sometimes when a question is too difficult for the Prime Minister, or when he does not want to answer, he responds with another question in kind. He responded by asking me a question on my party's stand on revenue-sharing. In other words, how would we split the pie, what would we do? I should like to take some time now to answer that question and, in so doing, deal with the government energy policy. I have described the minister as being like a boxer-kind of a fake to the left and still a few jabs from the right.
The Liberal policy is to raise oil prices and basically to give the industry the windfall profits. Canadianization is simply a clever ruse. Like many people, I think I have figured out, after going through the extensive document called "The National Energy Program," exactly how it works. The events of the last couple of days have confirmed my suspicions.
Large companies such as Imperial or Shell will issue more shares to Canadian investors so that they become "a Canadian company", thus eligible for those lovely and ample government handouts sprinkled throughout "The National Energy Program". Some of the Canadian companies that are now threatening to go on strike should read the program very carefully; they will find lots of handouts. Those large companies which will now have Canadian shareholders will still be controlled by foreign multinational oil companies. The government will be able to come to the House and say, "We have reached our goal-50 per cent Canadian ownership by 1990". The Toronto Star will be so happy, it will be ecstatic, but the situation will not really have changed.
Petroleum Administration Act
In other companies we will replace an American business elite with a Canadian one.
Hear, hear!

I hear my friends to the right applauding that. Is it really what they want? Apparently so, apparently the minister wants it as well. We will simply replace the Rockefellers with the Conrad Blacks or the Bob Blairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: With the T. C. Douglases.

Who will benefit? Who will pay? Let me talk about that for a moment. The average Canadian family will pay through increased costs for heating oil and increased transit costs. As a matter of fact, their costs for heating and transit will double in the next three years. The average family will be paying something like $350. To be more precise, to use the government's own estimates, they estimate that the cost of home heating oil will double in three years. On page 106 of "The National Energy Program" figures there show that the costs will go from $640 to $1,280 per year.
In my constituency the average family on an average street will find that they have to pay more to heat their homes with natural gas. They can expect a 30-cent per thousand cubic feet tax on their December bill. By 1984 the price of gasoline for the average family will double to $1,248 per year. That will mean a $100 per month increase for the average family. By 1989 it will cost $50 to fill their tanks with gas. The drive from here to Quebec City and back will cost $100.
I think ordinary Canadians feel that oil prices must go up. They know that. But this government has put up the oil prices without any cushion at all for the average family, and without any help at all for them.
I turn to the Prime Minister's specific question: how would we in the NDP share this revenue? "The National Energy Program" says that an overwhelming share of Canada's current oil and gas production was found prior to the rapid rise in world prices, which started in 1973. Therefore, we would further reduce windfall profits from these projects to the industry. There was talk about the split in the revenues being 45, 45, 10, which was the old split. The provincial government's share would be 45 per cent, 45 per cent would go to the oil companies, and 10 per cent to the federal government. What we would do is change the split totally. It would be more like 45 per cent to the federal government, 45 per cent to the province, and 10 per cent to the companies. If the government had any real guts, any real desire to get money back to the average person and away from the big companies, this is what they would do, too.
We would get even more money by developing the tar sands under public ownership. The large multinational companies want a 15 per cent to 20 per cent profit out of the tar sands, and the minister is prepared to allow them to receive that. Looking at the take from those tar sands I say to average Canadians and to the minister that it is not that difficult. Here

November 21, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
are the figures. If you raise it to $60, or $90 a barrel, as I believe it will rise to eventually, in 1990, multiply that by 140,000 barrels a day times 360 days over a period of 25 years and you will see the vast amounts of money that will be generated.
The minister is prepared to let the multinational oil companies develop those tar sands, and he confirms that in his energy policy. I am well aware of the difference between heavy oil and the tar sands. I remind the minister that people up there talk about the tar sands as being heavy oil as well. So there are vast amounts of money involved. That is our future up there in oil supplies and it looks now as if the government is prepared- $40 million Marc over there is prepared-to let the foreign multinationals develop that while at the same time giving the illusion that somehow this Canadianization will really help the average person.
I suggest we could give the money back to the people in a number of ways. One way to do this is obvious. It is by way of a cost of living allowance to families in order to get some cash right back to them so that they can keep up with the increased prices I have mentioned. Another method is to have a federal-provincial fund for energy development, not just a federal boondoggle, not a western development fund run by Ottawa bureaucrats for westerners but a genuine fund that will have federal and provincial co-operation.
I was in Vancouver last weekend where I was working in the municipal elections. I think Vancouver is very fortunate to have Mr. Michael Harcourt as the new mayor of Vancouver.
Is he a Conservative?

No, he is not a Conservative, I can tell you that. He is a proponent, and he was throughout the election- and this may have got him elected-of using some federal-provincial funds for rapid transit. In my city there is no rapid transit and we must get some funds there. There must be money for alternate energy. The people are ready for that.
Last night on my way home I was thinking about the minister giving $40 million to Imperial Oil, and he has put $20 million into the Enertech Corporation for alternate energy. He is willing to loan twice as much to Imperial Oil as he is prepared to put into alternate energy. Finally, money could be given to local citizens to set up neighbourhood energy programs where real conservation could take place at the local level, which is ultimately where these things must work.
Another point I wish to make in answer to the Prime Minister's question is that-

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Tell us what the price would be.

-we would take over the three largest foreign multinational oil companies under public ownership. We would set out a concrete commitment, not just this vague promise by the Liberals that something may happen in the future, but a concrete commitment with a timetable, and that could be paid out of future increases.
The minister asked me about oil prices. Yes, the price of oil would go up.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: How much?
The price of oil would go up.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: What is the reference?
I told the minister it would be 45, 45, 10.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Ten per cent would go to the oil companies, not the other way around, the way the minister talks about.
Mr. Speaker, instead of giving $9 out of $10 in public money to the private companies for drilling grants, as the program proposes, we would add an extra dollar to that and give all the money to Petro-Canada to do the drilling. Then the oil and gas that are discovered would be owned by the people.
Let me explain a little more. What this policy says is that if you are a fairly well-off taxpayer you can give $100 into a drilling fund, you will receive back $80 as a grant and you receive another $12 in tax write-offs. So $92 out of $100 is really paid for by the government. If the government will forgo that revenue why does the government not get something out of it? Why does it not get the ownership out of it? That, to my mind, would make sense as a policy.
As I said, we have been watching the government's words closely as compared with their actions. One of the actions taken was the Arctic pilot project. That is a new notion of government policy where gas will be taken by Petro-Canada and other companies from Melville Island in the western Arctic through the Northwest Passage down to a port in Quebec or Nova Scotia. That depends on which minister wins the battle for the port. The point is that the gas will then be exported to the United States. The boats that bring the product down will be foreign-built and manned by foreigners. Is that an industrial strategy as part of a national energy policy? It seems to me we have not changed anything if we continue with projects like that. That is one of the problems with this energy policy as it is set out.
Finally, there is no better example of the problem of resource sell-out than the pre-build of the pipeline. There it all is: short-term jobs and export of natural resources. And who benefits? The American multinational companies. What I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, is that if this Petroleum Administration Act is to be invoked-what I have called the War Measures Act of the oil war, if you like-then Canadians will want to see something in return. Canadians want to see a sparkling energy policy which would make the country selfsufficient and ensure that the ordinary Canadian benefits.

The "Baby Duck'' of oil.

In conclusion, there will be other speakers who will not speak in ignorance like my friend here next to me, but with some substance about energy in agriculture, energy in Atlantic Canada, about an industrial strategy tied to an energy policy, about gas exploration and gas exports. The Petroleum Administration Act is against our better traditions. Those traditions are based on co-operative federalism and on compromise. There are alternatives, but the Liberal government has refused to consider them. 1 have suggested some alternatives with regard to negotiation and dealing differently with the western provinces through a joint provincial-federal development fund.
This is the energy policy of our generation and it will be the crisis of the next five or ten years. To me this energy policy is like a Christmas present which, when it is unwrapped, turns out to be a gift to those who have always benefited. I refer to the business establishment in Canada. Although this time it is the Canadian business establishment, nonetheless, it is a policy that does not benefit the ordinary Canadian.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The hon. member referred to higher prices under his own scheme. Would he tell the House what he has in mind? Is it an international price, a percentage of the international price, or a price determined on Canadian costs?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. minister knows, I and my party have never agreed with the concept of moving to international prices. That is the OPEC price and it is an artificial price. Moving to the world price, which is the reason why my friends to the right lost the last election, would cause dramatic problems in Ontario and the other provinces in terms of layoffs and soon. Nevertheless, the price must move up.
We would like to see a made-in-Canada price, and I would remind the minister that it was my party which coined that term. This price would be a composite of the costs of production, reasonable profit for the companies and, of course, we would take extensive steps toward public ownership. This is the direction the government intends to take, but there would not be the extra cost and, therefore, prices could be held down somewhat lower than the minister suggests. The producing provinces would receive their fair share, which I think they are approaching now.
However, there would be more of a share for the federal government which, as I said in my speech, would be recycled quite dramatically and quite directly back to low and middle-income families who need the money because of increased costs.

Mr. Speaker, before I commence my remarks on the debate on the Petroleum Administration Act, I feel I have to respond to the very ill-founded comments made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). To slander my leader in the House when he is not here to answer is completely unforgivable.

I would like to turn to the debate at hand which is on the Petroleum Administration Act, with regard to the unilateral imposition of prices on oil and natural gas.
This particular portion of the debate is on the question of oil. Both clauses 36 and 52 of the Petroleum Administration Act provide for the unilateral imposition of a price if no agreement can be reached. We in the House must consider the impact of this imposition of establishing maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil as it relates to the conditions which prevail in the international market as well as to the probable effect it will have on the producers and consumers in Canada.
Both my friends from the New Democratic Party and representatives from our party have sought revocation of this price action. Before discussing the impact on the consumer and the producer, I think we should pause for a moment and consider why we are here. We should ask why we are having this debate. We should ask why this government was unable to reach agreement with the producing provinces prior to setting this unilateral price.
In December, 1979, our government was able to reach an agreement with the province of Alberta, after tough and protracted difficult negotiations, but we were able to reach agreement. The minister of energy for the province of Alberta has referred to this on many occasions, and the minister is very well aware of that. It has been the base from which they have negotiated in the province of Alberta. Let me remind the House that that agreement was reached after a series of difficult negotiations. Then the election happened. Since then we have had a display of attempts to reach some agreement between the two levels of government.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have been involved, but we have had no real documentation of the efforts of these two gentlemen in achieving agreement. On the other hand we have had a very full documentation from the minister of energy for the province of Alberta. He has outlined meetings he had with the minister on May 13, June 18 and 19, and later with the Prime Minister in July. Finally there were a couple of meetings in October. Mr. Leitch outlines in full detail the contents of the discussions and the negotiations which took place during the course of that time.
I am not here to claim that Mr. Leitch's recounting of these negotiations is the correct one, but it is the only one on the record. Today I set out a challenge to the minister to place on the record his version of the negotiations. Without that, we have only the one version. As long as that happens, the people of Canada and this House are going to be missing an important part of the negotiations which bear very directly on what we are talking about here today.
It is in the essence of any federation to deal and to compromise, to negotiate and to co-operate to reach agreement between the different partners. The essence of this legislation is that the federal and provincial governments must reach some agreement. In not reaching some agreement, they must display to the people of Canada an honest effort to reach agreement. Otherwise, the Petroleum Administration Act or this federation itself becomes a charade whereby the senior level of government, the federal government, can override the junior partners in confederation.
In place of the Petroleum Administration Act we have complete control by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and in place of a true confederation we have a centralist government here if this activity is allowed to continue further. If we have unilateral action on the price of oil, without any attempt at negotiations, I ask myself and I ask the House where do we go next? What is our next step? Where
November 21, 1980

will we next see unilateral imposition of the will of one level of government? Confederation is a partnership. We must take action based on compromise and conciliation. We must work hard at that in a country as diverse as Canada. Those agreements are not going to come easily. But attempts must be made in a serious and honest manner. Any unilateral action will seriously damage the fabric of confederation. We have seen today what is happening in the whole area of energy policy.
Over the past two or three months we have seen the same sort of action taking place in the constitutional debate. We cannot let this go on any further. This is the principal reason why we are here today debating this motion. In my opinion, the government is taking advantage of the Petroleum Administration Act to force its will on the people of Canada without making a proper effort at negotiation.
In order to support that statement I refer to a document, the infamous August 30 leaked cabinet document, outlining the negotiations leading up to the first ministers' conference on the constitution. At page 43 the statement was made:
The political climate in Canada is likely to be poisoned by a major energy conflict throughout the fall of this year and at least the early months of next year.
Clearly there was no expectation, and undoubtedly no efforts at achieving a satisfactory result in the energy negotiations. This act should only be used in the most unique and emergency circumstances when all efforts have failed, after serious efforts have been made, to seek agreement. Only when that has happened should this portion of the Petroleum Administration Act be invoked.
Let us now look to the impact of the act. That is what we were requested to do under the terms of the act in this debate. Consumers are being asked to pay SI more for a gallon of gasoline in the next three to four years. But what is the consumer getting for this $1 more? We know what the shortterm effects of that will be. The consumer will be paying vastly more, and most of it will be going into the coffers of the federal government. As I said before in this House, we see here a massive tax grab. When we compare what is attempted here under this energy policy with the policy which was set out by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), we see a tax grab which is fully three times as great as that in the December budget. That is a huge tax increase.
On this point let me just destroy a myth which has been allowed to grow over the last two or three weeks. The minister and the Prime Minister on many occasions have referred to the federal share rising from about 10 per cent or 11 per cent to 24 per cent. That statement is wrong. It is misleading. It is deceitful and it is dishonest. The percentage figure is far larger than that. Today there is no doubt the federal government gets about 10 per cent to 12 per cent of the revenues. Premier Lougheed has accepted the fact the federal government must gain a greater degree of revenue from energy in this country. But in the December budget the figure was going to move to 24 per cent.
Petroleum Administration Act
For the first little while after this budget came out I was scratching my head because I could not understand, with this far higher tax grab by this government, that we have seen the figure go up to only 24 per cent. Then I put the figures down on paper. It s not 24 per cent, the figure is about 48 per cent. The percentage figure is somewhere between 45 per cent and 50 per cent depending on the different assumptions you want to make. This has happened because the minister has conveniently left out the petroleum compensation charge and the Canadian equity ownership account charge, which will surely be drawn upon in the coming year. There are also some very unrealistic assumptions concerning the sale of natural gas to the United States, both in terms of price and volume. This has the effect of overstating the position which the industry and the federal government will be taking, as well as understanding the position of the provinces.
Let us hear no more of the 24 per cent figure. The figure is clearly of the order of 45 per cent to 50 per cent, which is fully double that in the statement. The people of Canada, when they heard this figure, said it was a reasonable policy. It is clear that we have a dispute today because the figure is far more than the 24 per cent that is set out in the program.
One other reason for the dispute today is that at the Prime Minister's press conference of July 25 he was asked what is a reasonable figure for the province of Alberta. He said, "We say that it would be fairer if Alberta reduced its take, say in the order of 40 per cent". The figure for the province of Alberta, again depending on assumptions, is somewhere between 30 per cent and 35 per cent. We have two sets of facts here. I say it is one set of facts and one set of fiction.
Let us look again to the impact on Canadian consumers and producers. The objectives of this program, some of which are set out specifically in the program, and some of which are implicit, are as follows. First, security of supply; second, Canadianization; third, economic development. Those are all mentioned quite specifically. Fourth, that any energy policy should work to bind this country together and not pull it apart. That should be a fundamental objective for all of the other three objectives as well.
How is this energy policy contributing to security of supply? We read of Mr. Lyons, the president of Ocelot Industries, saying, and I quote:
-Canadian exploration will be reduced and funds allocated to other projects.
Sulpetro, a good Canadian company, says "The program will reduce the company's cash flow, assets and availability to general explorations funds." Simmons Drilling rigs will probably be moved to the United States.
Just prior to question period this morning, I had a discussion with representatives of the Canadian Association of Oil Drilling Companies. They told me that 66 rigs will be moving to the United States over the next few months, 79 rigs have been idled through the cancellation of long-term contracts, and 50 additional contracts have been cancelled for winter drilling this month.

November 21, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
What is more far-reaching than this, because drilling contracts are a clear leading indicator of activity in the energy business, is that no commitments have been made for next summer. Around this time of the year the drilling companies normally expect to have about 75 per cent of their rigs spoken for. That is the state of confidence in the oil and gas industry today. It is reflected directly in the outlook for business for the drilling companies in this country.
1 have spoken to a number of other companies, some of which have not been quoted in the papers. There is a clear indication that we will be seeing less exploration funds, in some cases up to 50 per cent less, being spent in this country next year.
I ask the minister why he appears to have written off the conventional sources of oil in this country. About two years ago in west Pembina in western Canada, there was a very significant oil strike. It was in an area which had been drilled quite extensively and had been a very successful producing field. Rather than stay at the 5,000 foot level where the previous field had been found, the companies drilled down to about 10,000 feet and found the new west Pembina field. Therefore we should not be writing off conventional sources of oil in this country. Rather, we should be encouraging conventional exploration and development, and that is far from what is happening with this energy program.
I recall the 1973-74 period when we had the last major conflict between the federal government and the producing provinces. During that period we lost some very valuable time, about one full year, of exploration activity. A lot of rigs went south and spent their time finding oil in the United States. What is different between now and then is that our oil export versus our oil import balance is considerably different. We were in balance. At that time we were exporting about the same as we were importing. In fact at that time we had a surplus in our oil business of about $1 billion. Today we have a deficit of $4 billion. To lose this valuable time at a period when international oil prices are rising, exposes us to greater imports and greater uncertainty of supply. It is sheer folly, and will have a major impact on consumers in the years ahead.
To top it off, as the House well knows, this week we had the announced cancellation of the Cold Lake oil sands project, which has been resurrected on a short-term basis by a loan from the federal government. This is one of the most serious elements of the fallout from this very negative energy policy. The oil sands will be producing about 50 per cent of the oil requirements of the country in ten years' time. Those are the figures set out in the national energy program. They may well be producing to a greater percentage, depending on what happens with conventional oil discoveries, which are not very favourable at this time.
These projects take about six to seven years to bring on stream. With any delays, we risk losing all the good, talented Canadian people who will be drawn to similar projects in other countries. We stand to lose a tremendous amount of money through escalating costs of these programs if delays take place. It is only through agreement on the total conventional oil and
oil sands package that we will get the oil industry doing the job it should be doing, which is finding oil to improve security of supply in this country. Therefore, it is essential that we reach total agreement as quickly as we can.
Discussion of oil sands projects leads me to the next point, the question of jobs or economic development. One of the most serious effects of the delay of the oil sands projects is on economic development. We have seen, through figures which have been pulled together by major participants in both the Alsands and Cold Lake projects, an analysis of the total economic impact of the oil sands projects. Let me read this into the record.
The province of Alberta, depending on the calculation you use, will receive about 38 per cent to 42 per cent of the economic impact of these projects, the province of Ontario anywhere from 25 per cent to 28 per cent, the province of Quebec about 10 per cent, and other provinces somewhat less. The point is, and it is made clear by those figures, that the economic impact in Alberta is about equivalent to the economic impact that is felt and enjoyed by other provinces in this country, particularly Ontario and Quebec.
The Canadian Petroleum Association estimates that the impact of one Alsands development or one Cold Lake development will be close to $25 billion. About one quarter of that will go to the province of Ontario and another quarter to other provinces outside the province of Alberta. We in Ontario benefit through the purchase of iron and steel, metal fabrication and machinery. Also, high technology instrumentation and services are provided from this part of the country.
A number of other areas receive great benefit from activity not just in oil sands projects but also in other parts of the oil business in western Canada. Fahramet of Orillia received some major benefits through the sale of heat corrosion abrasive resistant castings used in the petrochemical industry. Simmons Drilling buys a vast number of its vehicles from eastern Canada, and if it is going to move its drill rigs south of the border, instead of going to Canadian manufacturers in Ontario and Quebec, that business will end up going to the United States.
A number of companies have reduced hiring projections for next year by as much as 50 per cent to 60 per cent. Grey-Mak Well Supplies, now the largest independent oil well casing manufacturer in Canada, has opened up a plant in the United States because it is concerned about the outlook for business in this country. There is no doubt that uncertainty, as well as the less attractive economics of the industry, have caused and will cause a great deal of economic unease and a turndown in business not just in western Canada but throughout this country, and it is to this that we must address ourselves when considering the impact on consumers, because many consumers will lose their jobs. Many will find that they will not work overtime hours.
Let me refer back to comments I was making about oil drilling companies. These companies move around many of the
November 21, 1980

small towns in Alberta, and they produce business not just in the oil drilling field but also in various aspects of the communities of western Canada. That is causing a great deal of uncertainty and, I might say, a great deal of anger with respect to what has happened to the business these people have enjoyed over the past few years. 1 am not referring to big, major companies, but to small corner stores, Harvey's hamburger type stores, and drycleaning stores. Those are the businesses which are being affected in western Canada by this energy policy.
I remind hon. members that 12 per cent of the total output of the Canadian steel industry is involved in supplying the requirements of the exploration and development industry in this country.
Another aspect, on the economic side of the national energy program we have before us today, is that most experts in the industry and on the periphery of the industry are projecting that we will be importing a larger amount of oil in the months and years ahead under this program. What does this mean in numbers we can all understand? It means that we will be spending Canadian dollars to buy oil from Saudi Arabia. We have seen what has been happening this week in Saudi Arabia. We will also be spending Canadian dollars to buy oil from Mexico and Venezuela. We import 425,000 barrels of oil a day. That translates into a figure of about $6.2 billion annually. However, looking at it from the standpoint of the individual, that works out to about $270 per person, or about $1,000 per family being spent outside this country to create jobs in Saudi Arabia, Mexico and Venezuela, but not here when we can be doing it right here in Canada.
The Bank of Montreal projected that in about five years that $6.2 billion figure will increase to about $11 billion to $16 billion. On a per person basis every man, woman and child will be spending $475 to $700 or, in terms of a family, $1,600 to about $2,500, to create jobs in other countries when we could be doing it here in Canada. That is opportunity lost. It means that jobs which are solely needed here, particularly when we are facing unemployment in the order of one million people this winter, are being exported to other countries.
What we have here in the national energy program is the worst of all worlds. As consumers we are paying high prices. We are paying one dollar more for a gallon of gasoline, but we are not getting economic growth or security of supply to offset that major cost. We are not seeing economic growth to offset the negative impact which will be felt. We are having deadweight high prices. They are not dynamic high prices which would create jobs in this part of the world.
I see that you are signalling to me, Mr. Speaker. I assumed that the time consumed by the frivolous points of order of members of the New Democratic Party would not be taken from my time.
