Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.
Let me comment very briefly on two other aspects of this policy. The first is Canadian ownership. We on this side of the House are very much in favour of increasing Canadian ownership of the oil and gas industry, and we were moving in that direction back in December.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: When? How?

This was back in December, 1979. It is very clear. The minister knows that. He should check with his officials. If he did, he would find out what we were doing. Canadian independents are very much weakened by this energy program. Multinationals can survive, but Canadian independents are being forced to go south of the border. The high taxes involved hit them harder than multinationals. In order that the government receives its 45 per cent to 50 per cent of the total industry revenue take, the government has hit independent companies much harder than it has hit the multinationals. That does not make sense to me. There has to be a better way. We just cannot afford to have these companies drawn away by much higher payouts. The netbacks on oil exploration are $9.50 in Canada versus $25. Those figures were quite clear before the budget, and the budget will widen the disparities between this country and the United States in the years ahead.
The overriding and chief objective any energy policy should have is Canadian unity. We must use energy policy to bring the east and the west together and not to drive them apart. The huge economic opportunity which is available through development of our energy reserves can bind this country together and lead to a tremendous burst of economic activity which would have a very positive effect and direct people away from any separatist tendencies and toward building this country to be a much stronger and viable one than it is today. However, the result of this policy will be that we will drive parts of the country away from each other.
The government is playing on divisions between the east and the west. Oil sands projects have been deferred, and that will lead to reduced economic opportunity here in eastern Canada. The energy policy can be a means of reducing western alienation. Let us not encourage it by taking actions which appear to attack different parts of the country without giving them a clear opportunity to have their voices heard in Ottawa through a proper series of negotiations, not the type of negotiations which appear to have taken place under the auspices of the minister.
In conclusion, let me say that there are five areas in which this energy policy is wanting: security of supply, job creation, Canadianization, a stronger Canada and-the part I was unable to cover-the very serious international situation. I urge that this House revoke the unilateral imposition of prices and force the government to return to the negotiating table with the province of Alberta and develop a policy which will be

Petroleum Administration Act
acceptable, because only through developing a policy which is acceptable to all parts of this country will we create the appropriate environment for the full development of our energy resources. Only then can Canada achieve its full potential as a strong country economically, secure in its oil supply and united in its purpose.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be participating in this debate today. Obviously I would have preferred it had the motions not been put forward, but since the two opposition parties have decided to put these motions forward, I am pleased that members on this side of the House will have a number of opportunities to speak again on this very important question of energy and to explain to the Canadian public the policy which is contained in the national energy program for the 1980s.
November 21, 1980

I am convinced that this debate will allow the government to obtain even more support for this program than it has had since the budget, and I must say 1 am very encouraged by the large degree of public support which has come from all areas of this country from ordinary people. I am not speaking here in particular about individuals who happen to occupy important positions, but rather about ordinary citizens on the street, families, farmers, fishermen, workers who drive to work, and people who provide for their family's needs. It is indeed encouraging that there should be a recognition in all areas of the country that what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and the government have announced in the budget and the national energy program appears to correspond to what the overwhelming majority of people in this country recognize as being a fair deal for all parts of Canada, a fair deal for the producing and consuming provinces and a fair deal for the consumers, even though the price of oil will rise.
Canadians are honest and mature enough to recognize that prices will have to rise, but they also recognize that the national government in the energy program has taken steps to try to cushion as much as possible the impact of those higher prices. Also, people recognize that this is a fair deal for the national government. What is recognized very clearly is the fact that never before has any Canadian government come forward with a declared intention to ensure that Canadians will have majority ownership and control of that strategic industry. The government has indicated its clear indication in this respect, and it is encouraging to see, not only a broad public support for this but recognition, even by industry, that it will have to adjust to this new reality in the years to come.
I want to indicate once more that the government will deal with this issue in a fair way but also in a determined way and we are convinced that this energy program is in the interest of Canadians all across this country.
Before embarking upon a discussion of the proclamations themselves, I should like to make one or two comments in relation to the speeches made by the previous two speakers. If the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) will allow me, I should like to raise with him a point about something he said regarding the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Trudeau). I listened with great interest to his speech and 1 found in it many good points which should be borne in mind, particularly his reference to Mr. Pearson's speech in 1964. But I think the hon. member's statement was unworthy of him when he referred to the present Prime Minister and his travels abroad.
What is he doing abroad?

speechtext: I think it is time that members of the House and Canadians in general grew up with respect to the role of Canada in international affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Every other country in the world would give their right arms to have a prime minister like the Prime Minister of Canada, to have a prime minister who honours his country in international fields as much as our present Prime Minister.
He should be here.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
As hon. members know, this country is dependent upon international trade. Indeed, we are dependent more than most other countries on international trade. Our country is a medium country; it is not a small country, but it is certainly not what one would call a super power. Under the leadership of people like Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Pearson and the present Prime Minister, our country has acquired great stature internationally and has grown on the basis of its expanding international trade. The activities of the Prime Minister, ministers and members of Parliament abroad are very important and significant in this respect.
I remind the hon. member that a number of Canadian businessmen are currently in Saudi Arabia negotiating a further enlargement of trade and business between Saudi Arabia and Canada. This means jobs and money for Canadians. It is important the government commitment is very clear in that respect. The country depends just as much for its jobs on what it sells abroad as it does on what it sells at home. Rather than making those comments, I think the hon. member should have applauded the initiative taken by the Prime Minister in visiting that country at the present time to help Canada expand its trade.
In addition, the hon. member knows Canada will be host next year to an economic summit of major economic powers of the western world. One of the items to be discussed at that time will be North-South relations, relations between the more affluent countries and the poorer ones. One of the most important problems in this very difficult issue is the role OPEC countries play in that respect. OPEC countries have become an immense centre of wealth, wealth which is being syphoned away from industrialized, underdeveloped and developing countries. The developing countries are suffering the most. If we want to make some progress on this issue which is very vital to not only the future of this country but the future of the world, it is essential we have the co-operation, support and willing participation of OPEC countries. At the present time this is recognized by people all over the world, except apparently on opposition benches. I say that with regret. I hope I am misreading the situation and that all parties of the House will support, with great enthusiasm and strength, the efforts the government will make and is making at the present time to try to achieve progress on an issue which is as critical for the future of the world as any we have known in the last several decades.
Therefore, I urge the hon. member and the people of Canada to look at the situation, not in a parochial manner, but to grow up and see what role Canada is called upon to play in the world nowadays. In that sense, when the Prime Minister of Canada is travelling abroad, he is speaking for the whole

November 21, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
country. We should be proud of it, like any other country in the world, when their heads of state or prime ministers are travelling abroad. I hope we will get this kind of support in the future.
I heard the hon. member indicate that the Prime Minister should be here, but I remind him that the government is going on, the country is going on, Parliament is going on.
He should be in Edmonton.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I hear the member saying he should be in Edmonton. As I said in the House earlier, Premier Lougheed indicated that he did not want meetings at the first ministers' level at the present time; maybe later on, but he feels they should be taking place at the level of officials. We have agreed to that, and those meetings will take place. I hope they will be successful. Perhaps there will be meetings at the ministerial level and most likely at the first ministers' level eventually. We have indicated that we are willing to have those meetings at any time, but there is no point in tying the Prime Minister to Ottawa and saying, "Just wait in case you are called to go to Edmonton". There has been a clear indication by the Premier of Alberta that he does not want this type of meeting at this time, and it is as simple as that.
I do not want to spend too much time on this particular point, but I thought it was important to stress it in light of the opening remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. Also I listened with great interest to the comments of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and those of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) respecting the necessity of co-operation and working on the basis of an agreement. We subscribe to those principles. We subscribe to the principles enunciated by Mr. Pearson as Prime Minister in 1964. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway indicated, the Prime Minister as a private citizen wrote something to the same effect-that it is essential, if this country is to survive, that there be co-operation between the levels of government. But obviously that co-operation must be a two-way street; there is no doubt about it. We have indicated in the past that we were ready to go to great lengths to make accommodation and to arrive at an agreement. In this particular instance we indicated that we wanted an agreement, that we preferred an agreement. Over the last six months we participated in many discussions.
You have not. That is false.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
We negotiated in good faith. At the end of this whole series of negotiations there was one offer made by the government of Alberta. It was made around August 1 by Premier Lougheed when he was in Ottawa. Even then we persisted and made other offers; we changed our plans as indicated in the budget; when it was obvious that we could not reach an agreement, we used the powers under the Petroleum Administration Act; and we indicated that as soon as an agreement could be reached, we would be willing and ready to rescind those proclamations in order to work on the basis of an agreement. Preferably this country must work on the basis of
an agreement, but there is also a responsibility upon the national government to speak for the whole country and to assume its responsibilities at particular times. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, among others, was saying that we should have had an agreement and that we should not have used this proclamation. But what does he propose? He proposes that instead we have a division of revenues between the levels of government of 45 per cent, 45 per cent and 10 per cent to the industry. He proposes that we have a made-in-Canada price that is not related to international prices. He also says there should be a federal-provincial fund, if I correctly remember, in which the revenues would be put together and divided. These are interesting proposals. But I tell the hon. member right now that there is no way the government of Alberta would agree to it. No way. It is also quite clear that the government of British Columbia would not agree. He should know that very well.
So what would he do? Would he use the Petroleum Administration Act and impose his will on those provinces because he cannot get an agreement? I tell him now he will never get an agreement from the governments of Alberta or British Columbia on the basis of the proposal he has put forward. One must be realistic in this respect and look at reality.
The hon. member for Etobicoke Centre said "Oh yes, that's great, we had an agreement last year in December." What about the poor independent member in the opposition in Edmonton who was thrown out of the Conservative party because he dared to say there might be something good in the federal constitutional proposals? That is a heresy of the worst sort in Edmonton these days. He was promptly kicked out of the caucus and his party because he breached the faith. Now he sits as an independent and ever since he has been in opposition he has tried unsuccessfully to get copies of any agreement, any memo, or any phone call recording any particular agreement with the Conservative government last year. He has not been able to get even one little sheet of paper.
I recommend to the member for Etobicoke Centre, since he has a short memory, that he take up for bedside reading a book published recently entitled "Discipline of Power" by Jeffrey Simpson. I suggest to him that he skip the pages in which reference is made to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) calling the Premier of Alberta his friend. 1 do not think that should go into the record. I recommend he read chapter seven, which is entitled "Limits of Loyalty". It goes into all kinds of detail about copies of memos sent and everything that transpired in those negotiations. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can tell me whether that chapter is wrong. The conclusion of the chapter is clear-that right up to the day of the budget on December 11 there were still phone calls between the prime minister and the Premier of Alberta, that a committee of officials proposed a new formula for the energy self-sufficiency tax and that Mr. Lougheed had inserted four other points to be clarified. We read that maybe an agreement could be signed, and maybe not. That is the last we heard
November 21, 1980

because, as we all know, the government was subsequently defeated. When the minister of finance came with his budget he had no agreement and as far as we know we could not find any record of any agreement anywhere except that there are some people who would like to rewrite history. Obviously, it would be great if they could rewrite it with the benefit of hindsight. Also, we can understand the reasons why they would like to rewrite it.
What is the situation at the present time? Action has been taken by the government to ensure that the price of oil and gas in this country will be firm over the next while, at least until there is an agreement reached with the government of Alberta and the other producing provinces. It spells out quite clearly what those prices will be, as was indicated at the time of the budget. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway says that is unprecedented. He says it is a drastic piece of legislation, a drastic action which should be used only in times of emergency and that we should have reached an agreement. I agree that we should have had an agreement. But it takes two to make an agreement, as he well knows. In order to make an agreement there must be willingness to compromise on both sides, otherwise you will be in a situation where one of the parties says, "You sign here, or else." We said we were trying, we did attempt to reach an agreement and it was not possible to do so. We have indicated we are still willing to talk. Let us keep this kind of measure in perspective.
Mr. Speaker, is this so unprecedented? We are setting the price monthly for the natural gas sold internationally. Every month the national government has an opportunity to modify the price at which we sell gas abroad. We set the prices at which we sell electricity abroad on the same basis. We set telephone rates across this country consistently. We set transportation rates for freight and innumerable items having to do with transportation, air transportation and rail transportation. We are also setting the price of wheat. We use the two-price wheat system as the hon. member knows very well. We also set the price for copper in this country. Around 1973 we had two prices for copper also. So what we have done at this time is to exercise what is clearly and fundamentally a power, a responsibility, that lies with the federal government. It lies with other federations in the world, not only with Canada. In Australia, the states own the resources in the same way as the provinces own the resources of this country. The national government in Australia sets prices for oil and gas constantly and systematically. They do not even do it on the basis of negotiation.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if the minister, in explaining the price-setting characteristics of his program, would permit a question at this time so that I might clear up something in my mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I would rather have the questions at the end of my expose. I do not like to use all the time at my disposal for questions and not be able to make a few more points I wish to make. If the hon. member wishes to ask me afterwards I will be very happy to answer him.
Petroleum Administration Act
What is being done here results from the fact that we could not get an agreement. Under the Petroleum Administration Act the power is quite clearly provided. As I indicated, it is done regularly and without question in a federal state like Australia. It is done in the same way by the national government in the United States. Therefore, I do not think we should consider that this is such an unprecedented step.
What does the opposition want? The opposition said we should rescind those proclamations. And then what? The price for this product would be decided by the government of Alberta for the whole of the country. We would have the government of one province in this country deciding on the price of a commodity traded interprovincially and internationally. I see a Conservative member opposite nodding his head. I say to him he does not know what the constitution of this country is. He does not know what this country is. We would end up in a situation where provinces determined, by government regulations, the price of commodities in interprovincial and international trade.
I challenge the provinces to name one other federal country in this world where the provincial governments or state governments have such powers. It does not exist, for the very good reason that if there is one country, there must be one common market and one national government which, if there is no agreement, must in the end make a decision and say that this will be the price. That is what has happened. The price has been set because we could not get agreement after six months of negotiations. However, in spite of that we are ready and willing to sit down again and talk with the government of Alberta. I am happy that Premier Lougheed has indicated that he is willing to see the discussions resumed.
The government was in effect forced to act in this particular instance. I remind the hon. member that in August the government of Alberta unilaterally raised the price of oil by $2. We looked in the other direction, if I may use that expression, at the time because the increase proposed by the Alberta government corresponded with an offer we had made in August. In order to gain some time in discussion and in order to allow for better relations, we decided to ignore that particular action, which could have been challenged, and let the price rise.
One week before the government introduced its budget, the government of Alberta proclaimed the Alberta Natural Gas Price Administration Act. The net result was that the Alberta government would control through regulations the price of natural gas coming out of the province. Since we were bringing down the budget, it was essential that the government assume and exercise its responsibility. I make no apologies for that. Indeed, we would have been remiss in our responsibility to the Canadian people had we done otherwise.
Therefore, we have proclaimed those actions under the Petroleum Administration Act. I hope negotiations will resume in the next short while and that we will arrive at an agreement.

November 21, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act

I would like to point out that it seemed to us extremely important in this whole matter that our decisions should take into account the interests of the various regions of the country and those of the consumers.
The proclamations now under consideration simply aim at implementing a pricing system for oil and gas sold interprovin-cially and internationally in this country. The price of gasoline sold in Alberta and gas produced and consumed in British Columbia will not be regulated by these proclamations. Only oil and gas shipped across provincial and international borders will be covered.
We wanted a pricing system which would be fair for the country as a whole. As hon. members are aware, this will result in significant net benefits for the producing provinces, and especially for Alberta. Under this program, the government of Alberta would receive within the next four years approximately $31 billion while British Columbia and Saskatchewan would, of course, receive much less since Saskatchewan would receive approximately $3.2 billion and British Columbia about $3.6 billion. Even so, these figures will seem fabulous to all the other regions.
As far as the consumer is concerned, we have endeavoured to take steps, so that even if prices were to increase in the coming years, he would be reasonably well protected or at least he could anticipate impending increases and then adjust his standard of living accordingly.
My hon. colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway has quoted figures from page 106 of "The National Energy Program" which I invite Canadians to get at their local post office. I am told that copies are available. Well, the hon. member will note that for the citizen of Winnipeg to whom he referred or for the citizen of St. John's, Newfoundland, for example, who spent about $680 for heating in 1980, should he convert his heating system to natural gas or take advantage of all benefits under the energy conservation schemes available under the national energy program, the heating bill of that citizen in Winnipeg will be reduced from $680 to a potential cost of $535 in 1984, while for the citizen of St. John's, Newfoundland, it could be reduced from $810 to $760 through the necessary conservation measures.
I mentioned Winnipeg and St. John's, Newfoundland, but I could also mention every other Canadian city. This means that Canadian consumers are invited to play a real part in this endeavour to attain energy self-sufficiency during the next decade. In addition, the program clearly indicated that even if prices rise, Canadian consumers will be in a position to protect themselves thanks to the programs which we have made available to them.

I notice that I have only a few minutes left. I would have loved to have spent more time putting forward other aspects but I understand we will have an opportunity to have a second
debate in the next few days on the second proclamation. I may want to use that opportunity to come back to the points which have been raised already in this debate and to cover several more points.
It is important to note that the government has made genuine, serious efforts to resolve this particular issue over the last few months. We have discussed a pricing formula and we have offered to abandon, if necessary, the existing mechanism for pricing and offered a new equalization formula whereby the provinces would have a more equal share amongst themselves. But those proposals were turned down. We tried to separate the issues of the tar sands and heavy oil from the issues of conventional oils, but that was turned down also. We proposed that there be a tax on the export of gas and electricity, but that was turned down. The budget was changed at the last minute and that plan was abandoned in order to accommodate the views of the producing provinces, particularly the government of Alberta.
Unfortunately, up until now, our proposals have not been fruitful. These proclamations have been introduced as a stopgap measure and as a substitute for the lack of an agreement. We indicated that we are undertaking further discussions without preconditions. I stress that this government has set no conditions for these further discussions. I ask the opposition parties to observe who is setting conditions and asking for certain requirements ahead of time.
It is important that we achieve a resolution which will ensure to the federal government a fair share of the resource revenue while ensuring for the producing provinces an increase in wealth to the extent they would never have dreamt of ten years ago or even as recently as five years ago, while still leaving enough profit for the industry. As a national government, we must think of the national interest. The national interest of this country is obviously larger than the interest of a particular region or province. We are determined to do everything we can to reach agreement. Again, 1 say to members on both sides of the House, because I know that many of them are as concerned as we are, and rightfully so, about the deep disagreement existing at this time, that I hope the debate in the country and particularly in Alberta will be kept at a level of reason with reasonable arguments. There are so many arguments being used which have no foundation at the present time. I invite the Tory member on the other side who is so vocal at the present time to keep his cool and listen a little bit because he might learn a thing or two. It might be helpful, instead of telling his constituents what he has been over the past little while-
Name one.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: -to use his head and advance a resolution to this problem rather than fan divisions in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to pose a question to the minister. It concerns the proclamation of section 36 in the Petroleum Administration Act. I believe the government had two possibilities. First, to invoke and set the price of oil for one year and then hope that negotiations with the producing provinces would continue to affect the price subsequently.
The second alternative of the federal government was to invoke this section of the Petroleum Administration Act to set a schedule of pricing over a period of years from five to ten years, or four to ten years, in other words, set a pricing structure which then acts as a major club on the producing provinces in terms of the possibility of reaching agreement or no agreement at all.
Could the minister clarify very carefully if possible whether the invocation of this section of the act is for a period of one year only so that if an agreement is reached with the producing provinces within this year, then we will not have this act in place? If the government needs to come forward with this act again a year from now, it will come before Parliament again to invoke it. It is important that I know the answer to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the point raised by the hon. member. He knows that we did come forward with a ten-year program called the national energy program. He knows, too, that the budget itself announced the projection of prices over that long period. I am sure the hon. member knows also that the industry and the people of Canada generally have been clamouring for some certainty. There have been consistent protests over the last few years because it was very difficult, if not impossible, to plan, especially for megaprojects on the basis of what the price is this year when we do not know what it will be two years from now or four years from now. In other words, some certainly was needed as to the future.
It was to ensure a certain degree of certainty and clarification as to the government's policy that it was decided to put forward this long-term plan. We have indicated that this is a ten-year program. It would be naive or irresponsible to say that in a ten-year program not one iota can be changed, or that this is cast in stone, just like the Bible. So that is not our perception. However, we have put forward the proclamation in question in order to avoid as far as possible-and I hope we will reach an agreement eventually-this kind of annual mutual harassment and this annual dramatic time which industry and governments have to go through when month after month they have to come back to renegotiate a pricing regime. We have put forward a pricing regime which we think will be fair for the industry over the next ten years and for the various regions of the country.
The government of Alberta has indicated that it is willing to sit down again and look at this issue, and so have we. It is there for everybody to see. I would think from my conversations with the government of Alberta and the government of Saskatchewan that they themselves would prefer, if possible, to
Petroleum Administration Act
have a resolution which would be for more than one year so that government and industry can get down to the business of finding more oil and gas and making more money and jobs for everybody.
Mr. Speaker, in rising today to speak on this important subject-

Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a point of order? Please excuse me but I thought the hon. member was rising on a point of order and I hesitated to disturb him. The minister said he would answer short questions. Might I put one to him? It concerns the invocation of the act and it is fairly short. Might I do that before the hon. member begins to speak?

I thank the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), Mr. Speaker.
1 do not think the minister would get disagreement from this corner of the House that in the end, in an emergency, the national government must make a decision and take action. But 1 would remind the minister that under our constitution the provinces have power over resources. I would think that he, as a Quebecker, would be very much aware of that. My question is this: there did not seem to be a dispute, in the eyes of the average Canadian at least, with Alberta in terms of prices. The minister mentioned that the province of Alberta had raised the price by $2 a barrel and the federal government had not opposed that. However, there was no indication that it would be raised any further. That being the case, could the minister not have said to the province of Alberta: "Here is our scheme and our maximum limits; if you go above that, then we will bring in the act, but as long as there is no dispute now, there is no reason to invoke this act." Would the minister explain to me why he did not go along with the present situation without invoking the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
At the time I had discussions with my colleague in Alberta there was agreement that there would be no price increase after August 1 above $2 until October. But the government of Alberta was retaining its right to act after that. As I indicated one week before the budget, the government of Alberta decided to proclaim the Alberta Gas Marketing Act, the Alberta Natural Gas Price Administration Act.
The hon. member must realize that the Minister of Finance needed to bring in a budget. In every country in modern times energy is a fundamental element in determining budget policy. For instance, it must be determined how much money a government will need in terms of support for energy programs-whatever they are in each country. Therefore, it was impossible to ask the Minister of Finance to walk into this House and say, "Here is a budget, but assuming that nothing else happens over the next little while, this is approximately what it will be". I think the hon. member's party would have been the first one to rise in protest and outrage. It would be

argued that by failing to disclose his plan of action the Minister of Finance was not assuming his responsibility; it would be argued he should ask Parliament to vote on something definite, not on something hypothetical and dependent on the goodwill of other levels of government which are not answerable to this House but to another constituency. Mr. Speaker, I rise today very bitter and very deeply angered as a member of Parliament from western Canada who sees an issue that is before the Canadian people which creates a division that is unnecessary. It begins with premises that are true and reaches conclusions that are false.
We do not have an energy crisis in this country. We have enough coal to supply petrochemical needs for 300 years. We have in the oil reserves of western Canada enough supply for several hundred years. What we lack in this country is a systems policy, not energy. The energy is there. There is a struggle between the federal government and the provinces. With the tactics they are using against the will of those who want to put systems in place, they are destroying the fabric of this nation, the will of those at the grassroots to make a commitment to energy security. Even with our abundance of coal, which is the envy of the world, we have a struggle of politics going on which is not only denying Canadians energy, but causing an excessive loss of jobs and capital as well.
I use the example of one tar sands plant. If one plant were to close and to stay closed for the projected life of the project, it would involve a loss of some $290 billion to Canada. That is what is involved in the ripple effect through the Canadian system. Of that amount, 40 per cent would go into the province of Ontario. There would be an enormous loss of jobs, not in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia but in consequence of the raping of central and eastern Canada against its security of supply, the assurance that there will be oil and petroleum products for the driving of cars, heating of homes and the industrial sector.
I wish to place on record what it would mean if Alsands were to receive its full documentation and endorsement from the federal government. It would put some $800 million into
the province of Ontario in the area of iron and steel production, $370 million for the fabrication of machinery in the manufacturing basin of central Canada, $325 million into Ontario for other forms of manufacturing and processing, $740 million into Ontario and Quebec in relation to financing through banks, trust companies and the like for capitalization of these megaprojects. It would involve another $370 million in trades and services and an additional $7 million in spill-over effects with regard to employment.
I become very annoyed when I hear the tone of the debate which tries to create the impression that there was a disagreement and an inability to work out with the province of Alberta an energy package, leaving Canadians in a desperate position. The truth is there was never a serious attempt by the present federal government to deal with the province of Alberta. The Alberta energy minister said the first two occasions there was a visit from representatives of the federal government it was a milk and cookies occasion, a get acquainted party. There was never a document on the table, never a discussion, never a piece of paper in front of them.
When the minister comes before Parliament and recounts the number of times he went from Ottawa to Edmonton or someone came from Edmonton to Ottawa, he wants Canadians to believe those were negotiations and that, because there was no resolution, Alberta failed. The truth is that since being re-elected last February, the federal government has not placed one proposal before the province of Alberta. With their sinister attitude, they try to create the illusion that they are being denied an agreement after all the efforts they made. The truth is otherwise. Their first two missions were simply to get acquainted with the staff of the two energy departments.
This proclamation is before us because the minister said an agreement could not be reached. He further said it was not the federal government which was placing conditions on the negotiations. That is a rather sinister view when you think of the conditions Alberta is placing on this. The province of Alberta is saying that if you are going to deal, you will deal with us on the question of petrochemical energy. We have seen the tactics of this government.
During the last first ministers' conference, a document was leaked indicating that the province of Alberta should be divided from the other three western provinces, that it should be isolated. They wanted to create an enemy at which the other provinces could point. With regard to the Atlantic provinces, they wanted to isolate Newfoundland from the other maritime provinces so it could be pointed at as the enemy.
What are they doing in their energy negotiations? They are trying to separate tar sands oil. Why? When that is removed from the negotiations, they can of their own free will do what they want with the energy package. Obviously in their negotiations Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have every right to say to the federal government that if it wants to talk energy, come and do that, but if it wants to divide up the pie, go home. They have every right to tell them to go home if they are not bargaining fairly. The minister comes here lily white
November 21, 1980

and clean, stating that it is the provinces which are making the conditions. I agree, they are putting on a condition. The condition is, if you cannot bargain fairly, don't bargain at all.
Then what do we find? We find the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) spending 40 days and 40 nights in the dessert of Arabia. For what purpose? For $40-a barrel oil.
The truth is that since he was elected he has spent more time in the Middle East than he has spent in the province of Alberta. Elon. members opposite try to put forward the view that we will not negotiate. What an unfair and sinister position for a government which will not take the time within the provinces of its own country that it takes in dealing with energy matters on some foreign soil.
I see that the time is up, Mr. Speaker. May I call it four o'clock?

Income Tax Act
bank, trust company or encashing agent must retain 25 per cent of the interest coupons and remit them to the Minister of National Revenue. There that interest collected shall be deemed to have been levied and paid or shall be available for the person involved to apply in a subsequent taxation year for reimbursement. However, there is a "Catch 22" aspect to this in that it is a requirement of another section of the Income Tax Act passed in 1966 that every income tax return shall contain a social insurance number and that the income tax authorities are empowered to reject such a return unless completed in a form satisfactory to the taxation authorities.
This meant that an elderly person who did not have a social insurance number or a child of 12, for example, who owned some Canada Savings Bonds by way of gift or any other means was not able to cash interest coupons and recover their value because that person did not satisfy a bureaucratic requirement with regard to social insurance numbers. There are a few members in this House who were present in 1964 when the late Prime Minister Pearson solemnly stated in this House under questioning that social insurance numbers would not be used for any purpose other than for social security reasons. In fact, he answered questions of the former leader of the opposition, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, particularly on the subject of income tax, and he denied it would be used for income tax purposes.
The first thing that happened was that in 1966 there slipped through-not surreptitiously or anything; I suppose in the press of events-a requirement that for identification purposes the social insurance number would be required on every tax return of a private individual. That should have been an alert, but unfortunately too many people somehow or other took it to be a reasonable request. However, that was only the opening of a door.
Since that time there have been requests for social insurance numbers by department stores when applications for charge cards were made, by oil companies for credit cards, by the Department of External Affairs for passports and by any number of other organizations, including midget hockey teams. Recently I learned that in the province of Alberta a government department was requesting social security numbers for children in a musical group, all about the age of 12, who were going to travel outside the province on a government grant. Fortunately, after one telephone call the minister in charge of that department decided that this was a lot of bureaucratic nonsense and reversed that decision right on the spot. There has been abuse. Is this country going to accept the principle that everyone must have an Orwellian identification number? The armed services got away from their district service numbers allowing one to identify what kind of serviceman a particular individual was, whether he belonged to an eastern district or whether he was in the army, the navy or the air force, by substituting social security numbers. 1 object, and so do my colleagues. I know that the hon. member for Well-ington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), formerly the minister of state for the Treasury Board, had indicated he was going to

November 21, 1980
Income Tax Act
introduce legislation restricting the use of social security numbers.
Elowever, that did not come to pass. In November, 1979- and my colleague from Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) will elaborate on this-the previous administration indicated there was to be a study on their use. That was affirmed and extended by the present administration. The report should have been in by November 1. It has not been tabled. It may have been made to the government, but it has not been tabled.
In any event, I have, through clause 1, moved to delete those two subsections. They are amplifications of the original section 234 dealing with ownership certificates, but in addition to the ownership certificates there was the question of the social insurance number. It was a stupid thing because the minister of the day tacitly admitted that if the person concerned wanted to give any sort of social security number, whether his, hers or someone else's, it did not matter. So long as there was a number, the banks and cashing agents did not have to withhold anything. When and if a cross audit would catch up with it, God only knows. Since that time several of the banks have indicated that they will not abide by those regulations, and they are not doing so. If the section is being disregarded, it is in disrepute, and the only thing to do is to strike it from the record. I am sure the present administration will decide to strike it from the record in the Income Tax Act. So I hope that hon. members can support that aspect of it.
Now with regard to section 237, it has to do with a failure to show a social security number on an income tax return which need not be then accepted by the income tax authorities. So far as I am concerned, if I have a social security number and I voluntarily put it on my tax return, that is my business. It is my number for my private use. Since when has income tax been part of social security?
Therefore, when I move to strike 237(1) and 237(2), I do away with the obligation and necessity. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has not indicated anywhere in her legislation that an individual has to apply for a social security number. But section 237 of the Income Tax Act says one has to do so. The provision has become distorted. It has become a case of the tail that wags the whole dog. The initiative is now with the Department of National Revenue to decide who shall apply for a social security number, and 1 move to strike that out. However, my colleagues wish to discuss this matter further.
I want to turn now to something that as a lawyer 1 find dastardly and absolutely wrong. I gather that a similar feeling is felt by the council on uniform legislation, or a like body, in that, under section 239, the Crown may move either by way of indictment or by way of summary conviction if there is to be prosecution of an offence under the Income Tax Act. The decision as to whether it will be by indictment or by summary conviction is made by the Attorney General of Canada, not by the minister of national revenue, which, in effect, means it is
the director of public prosecutions who makes the recommendation to the deputy attorney general, and that is the authority. Unfortunately, offences under section 239 against the Income Tax Act include a false return or an evasion of a return and destruction of records, the disposal of books, acquiescence or collaboration in the making of false returns, all the offences one can think of under the Income Tax Act including one which is so general that there is no way of escaping it, namely, "wilfully or in any manner evading or attempting to evade compliance with this act or payment of taxes imposed by this act." That is, in fact, a difference of opinion with the taxing authorities. If I have a difference of opinion with the taxing authorities and I say that I will not pay those taxes, that is my interpretation and I am "wilfully or in any manner" attempting to evade payment of taxes imposed by this act. The taxing authority says that the act imposes these taxes, and I say, no, I am evading that by my interpretation. That is a wilful act and I am then guilty of an offence. In addition to any penalty provided, I am liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than 25 per cent or to a fine and imprisonment. But subsection (2) says:
Every person who is charged with an offence described by subsection (1) may, at the election of the Attorney General of Canada be prosecuted upon indictment and, if convicted, is in addition to any penalty provided, liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years and not less than two months.
That means the judge has no option. In practice it means that if the director of prosecutions decides that the Crown attorney will move by way of an indictment and there is a finding of guilty, or even an admission of guilt because often the facts are there, a mandatory jail sentence is imposed regardless of how severe or otherwise the judge considers the offence to be. That is wrong. We throw too many people into jail as it is. It is the court which should decide whether or not a person goes to jail, not a functionary of the Department of Justice. My amendment gives scope to the judge on the penalty and it is the judge who will decide. There is none of this business of going by way of indictment. Gracious me, there is a section in the Bank Act which provides for prosecution by way of indictment. I wanted to strike it out but was told that a recommendation would come forward for the government to do away with proceedings by way of indictment under these acts. This is not the Criminal Code. It is a civilian act along with the Bank Act. It is civil statutory law. We have to take a much more civilized and just stand. This business of moving by indictment is subject to abuse. Political motivation may determine that a certain individual will go to jail. We have seen occasions where the choice of whether the government moved by way of indictment or by way of summary conviction seemed to be based upon political capriciousness. If somebody desires to get even with a certain prominent citizen, to make an example of him, or just to get at him, he can move by way of indictment. His crime may be no worse than that of the neighbour down the street who lives at a much lower profile. One will be subjected to proceedings by way of summary conviction and the other by way of indictment. They are no more than offences against statutory law, and that section should be repealed.
November 21, 1980

Many hon. members have not been exposed to this particular facet of our statute law, so I commend it to them. Often within the confines of private members' hour anomalies or injustices in various statutes are pointed out to fair-thinking people, and parliamentarians, as fair-thinking people, say we must do away with them. It is in this spirit that I offer this legislation to my colleagues in the House of Commons, so that they will accept it in the spirit of fair-mindedness toward their fellow men, and do away with these anomalies, injustices and in so far as the social insurance is concerned, some rather silly results.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the bill presented by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), I should like to begin by paying tribute to his motives in bringing to the attention of the House what he considers to be anomalies in existing legislation. His motives deserve the recognition of the House, but as I think he will see in a moment, in several respects there are real differences between his approach and his understanding of the income tax amendments and mine.
Bill C-228 proposes three amendments to the Income Tax Act. One of them does not require any extensive discussion, that is, the first clause of the bill to repeal subsections 234(5) and (6) of the act. Those are the sections which relate to persons cashing bearer coupons, warrants for interest and dividend payments without listing their social insurance number on the ownership certificate. Where this number is not given, the person paying the interest or dividend must deduct 25 per cent of the amount as a withholding tax. This deduction is credited against the recipient's personal income tax owing for the year.
Repeal of the subsections to which the hon. member referred was in fact proposed in the notice of ways and means motion tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on April 21. It is simply unnecessary to pass Bill C-228 in order to abolish that provision.
However, the other two proposals in this bill require closer examination. Both suggest a willingness to weaken the integrity of the tax system and leave it open to abuse and fraud. We all realize that throughout history the tax collector has never been a popular figure. It has always been easy to score political points by offering to weaken the tax system, but I suggest this can be a dangerous and self-defeating game. We must recognize that income tax is more than just a means of raising federal revenues. It is an important aspect of the whole effort of government to promote social justice through redistribution of income, support for the needy, and the development of the less prosperous areas of Canada. This is what is at stake when we consider the need to protect the integrity of the tax system.

speechtext: Would the hon. parliamentary secretary accept a question?

Yes, Mr. Speaker.
Income Tax Act

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: I know the parliamentary secretary is giving a philosophical justification for income tax, but perhaps he would go back to its origin and say that it was a special war tax. Until 1948 it was known as the income war tax act, merely to raise funds to pay for the expenses of war. How does he reconcile that tax with the support of our social system?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Of course the hon. member is correct in drawing to the attention of the House the fact that when income tax was first introduced in the United Kingdom, prior to and during the First World War, it was regarded by some as a temporary measure. I thank the hon. member for inviting my comment in this regard. Since then, the liberal philosophy, of caring for each other through collective measures which require revenue, whether raised in the form of income tax, corporate income tax or capital gains tax, has become well established in the practices of all democratic nations. Of course Canada is no exception in that regard.
Income tax is more than just a means of raising federal revenues. At least we on this side of the House see it as the principal method of achieving the balance of social justice and equity to which we subscribe. Fundamentally that is what is at stake when we consider the need to protect the integrity of the tax system.
When we consider that clause 3 of the bill would eliminate the present legal option of proceeding against serious tax evaders by way of indictment, we see some problems arise immediately. The hon. member for Edmonton West objects to empowering the Attorney General of Canada to decide on an indictment proceeding instead of proceeding by way of summary conviction. He objects to the minimum sentence of two months in jail which the law provides for those persons convicted. The hon. member discussed this same issue at some length during the 1971 debate on the tax reform bill and again in 1973 when he presented a private member's bill on this subject. I suggest that he is no more likely now than he was then to win majority support in the House for his approach.
We are talking about measures to deal with serious income tax fraud, not just any minor attempt to evade tax payment. The kind of offences we are considering are set out in Revenue Canada's information circular on tax evasion and tax avoidance. It describes some of the factors which are considered as grounds for deciding to proceed by way of indictment. It is clear that we are talking about serious attempts at tax evasion by people who are second offenders, people who sell their assets or move them out of the country to escape the collection of taxes owing, people who intimidate others to help in tax evasion schemes, people who counsel others on tax evasion practices, people who have evaded substantial amounts of tax owing. These are some of the factors that must be considered.
If any member seeks proof that we are discussing exceptional cases, I would point to the Revenue Canada statistics which show that over the six years prior to last March 31 only 12 taxpayers have been imprisoned through indictment proceed-

November 21, 1980
Income Tax Act
ings. So the decision by the Attorney General to proceed by way of indictment is clearly not one taken lightly or routinely.
It is not a rare or remarkable situation for the Crown to be empowered with the option of proceeding by way of either summary conviction or indictment. The Criminal Code has many such instances. Agreed, it is not customary for this provision to be coupled with a mandatory jail sentence for convictions on indictment. But 1 submit that it is justified in cases such as this.
The sponsor of the bill has argued in the past that the law really means that the Attorney General of Canada has power to send someone to jail by proceeding by way of indictment. This argument conveniently overlooks the fact that it is still the court which decides whether an offence has been committed and whether conviction is warranted.
Serious tax fraud is one of the so-called white collar crimes. It represents an effort by more prosperous persons with substantial tax liabilities to evade payment of their taxes. There is a view held by some that white collar law-breakers should receive lenient treatment in the law. That cynical view would be confirmed if Parliament decided to drop this provision in our laws. The possibility of a mandatory jail term-even one of only two months-must serve as a powerful deterrent for those who might seek to defraud the treasury in this way. Too often a fine is regarded merely as a cost of doing business.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss briefly the third proposal in the bill now before us. It would end the requirement for taxpayers to report their social insurance number with their tax return. It is difficult to see what such a step would accomplish, apart from weakening Revenue Canada's ability to collect income taxes that are owing and to ensure the fair and efficient administration of the Canada Pension Plan and the unemployment insurance system.
The advent of electronic data processing has opened up a whole new world of concern to many people. Large quantities of information about individuals can be stored in various computer data banks. One of the chief concerns about the social insurance number is that it might be a handy key which would allow the pooling of information about an individual from a number of these data banks without his knowledge or consent. However, the problem here is not really the social insurance number. Computer technology allows the linkage of information without using the SIN-for example, by using name, address or birth date. The SIN is a handy target for criticism, but the real issue is the problem of data linkage itself. Our concern should really be with that, and not with the secondary issue of the social insurance number.
Under part IV of the Human Rights Act proclaimed on March 1, 1978, Parliament established a method for controlling the unauthorized exchange of personal data in federal information banks. Perhaps these provisions can be strengthened. Certainly more should be done about the data banks on individuals which exist in the private sector and how this information can be used.
There is legitimate concern about the proliferating use of the social insurance number in a wide variety of applications that do not relate to the administration of social security programs and the tax system. But none of these problems is met by the proposal to exclude use of the SIN from income tax returns, and much would be lost by this proposal, which would weaken Revenue Canada's ability to carry out its responsibility to protect the integrity of the tax system. We must remember, too, that information from individual tax returns is used to establish the individual's rights under the Canada Pension Plan and to determine insurable earnings for purposes of the unemployment insurance program. Mr. Speaker, both of these programs depend on the social insurance number. If the SIN cannot be used on income tax returns it will simply compound the number of information returns that Canadians will have to make to the federal government. The administrative cost and the nuisance would be multiplied.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on his pursuit of his private member's Bill C-228. I would like to read the explanatory note which sets out why there is cause for concern. It states:
The purpose of this bill is to repeal certain provisions of the Income Tax Act relating to social insurance numbers, and the consequences of failing to obtain such a number for entry on tax returns. At present, there are thousands of Canadians who do not possess social insurance numbers.
The parliamentary secretary did not address himself to that part of the bill. As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, it was a bureaucratic decision that implemented this in the first place and this afternoon we heard a bureaucratic answer. It was not something that was compiled by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) at all. This bill calls attention to the serious consequences that a taxpayer faces with the abuse of the SIN number. When the SIN was introduced in 1964 it was not meant for this purpose. There is legitimate concern about government abuse of the SIN.
The Conservative government, in a release dated November 26, 1979, took positive action in this area. That release stated:
Finance Minister John Crosbie and Revenue Minister Walter Baker announced today that the government intends to drop the requirement that persons cashing bond coupons must provide a social insurance number or pay a 25 per cent withholding tax.
The minister of justice in the Clark government, in a release dated February 1, 1980, announced that he had ordered a special study by Canada's Privacy Commissioner on the use of social insurance numbers. This study was continued under the present government. On May 23, 1980, they announced that the scope of the special social insurance numbers study by Canada's Privacy Commissioner would be expanded to include those federal government institutions to which part IV of the Human Rights Act applies. We were to have received this report on November 1. I hope it will be tabled very shortly.
Obviously the government of the day was concerned about what was happening about the abuse of social insurance numbers or they would not have continued the study and
November 21, 1980

extended it for another three months. Concern has certainly been expressed by Canadian citizens over the past number of years about the abuse of the SIN by government departments and invasion of privacy. As the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, children are now required to submit a social insurance number when they register to play football and hockey. That is a lot of darned nonsense. I hope the report will make recommendations to put a stop to that.
To show how difficult it is to send a letter to a serviceman, a recent article stated, "It may take SIN to get that card to a serviceman". Apparently, if his social insurance number is not on there he might not receive his Christmas card. Mr. Speaker, what kind of nonsense is that? I hope the government study which should have been completed by November 1 will be available to all members in the very near future. I hope it will eliminate nonsense of this kind, about the need to put a social insurance number on a Christmas card.
A former prime minister, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, spotted the problems with the SIN back in 1964. He asked questions of the House leader at that time. He wanted an assurance for the Canadian people that any information provided in the social insurance number application form would be maintained on a completely confidential basis and would not be used for any other purposes or passed over to any other department. The Liberal House leader at the time replied that the information would be maintained in Ottawa for government purposes including the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the proposed Canada Pension Plan.
The right hon. gentleman repeated his question adding that the system bears a strange relationship to dictatorship. Certainly, the system has expanded from its original purpose back in 1964. Also, at that time we found out that the RCMP had told a commission in Ottawa that the little white plastic card bearing each taxpayer's social insurance number has evolved into an identification card and is vital to the RCMP. The RCMP was given direct access to social insurance data held by the Unemployment Insurance Commission in 1969.
Just five years earlier, the government managed to get the social insurance number established in law by promising never to let it be used for any purpose other than the necessary clerical work associated with the social insurance system. I hope the government report which was to be completed by November 1, 1980, covers these aspects and outlines plans to stop abuses of the SIN as pointed out by the former Conservative prime minister, and the hon. member for Edmonton West. Perhaps the last government speaker will indicate to the House today whether this report was, in fact, completed on November 1, and, if so, when hon. members of the House will be able to obtain a copy.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill introduced today by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has commendable aspects, but the government has certain
Income Tax Act
concerns, and 1 would like to address my remarks to those concerns.
This bill proposes three distinct amendments to the Income Tax Act and although they differ in subject matter, all three have a common thread. They all relate to methods of protecting the integrity of the tax system, methods of ensuring that each of us pays his proper tax. One deals with a withholding tax on interest and dividend payments, another with legal recourse against serious cases of tax evasion, and the third with the use of the social insurance number in administering the tax system.
I should like to address most of my lemarks to the latter point, which proposes to abolish the requirement for taxpayers to list their social insurance number on their income tax returns. But before that, I should discuss briefly the other two proposals in the bill.
I do not expect there will be much disagreement with the first clause of the bill. It would do away with the requirement that 25 per cent of interest and dividend payments being paid by means of bearer coupons or warrants must be withheld whenever the recipient does not list his or her social insurance number on the ownership certificate at the time of payment. A similar change has been proposed in ways and means motions both by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and by his predecessor. Obviously, the original purpose of this withholding tax was to ensure that income tax liabilities on bearer bond coupons and similar transactions were met. If finance ministers of two different governments agree that it is not necessary, then I suspect it will not be greatly missed.
Clause 3 of the bill, however, has a good deal less to recommend it. By this clause, the sponsor of the bill seeks to remove from the Income Tax Act a legal sanction which is now available for dealing with serious cases of tax fraud and evasion. Under this sanction, the Attorney General of Canada has the option of proceeding in the courts by way of indictment against accused tax offenders, rather than proceeding by way of summary conviction. For persons convicted on such an indictment, the law provides a mandatory prison term of between a minimum two months and a maximum five years.
As I understand it, there are precedents in the Criminal Code for the Crown to proceed by way of indictment, rather than the more customary summary conviction route, in serious cases of lawbreaking. If the Crown were to have frequent recourse to this provision, using it not only for major tax frauds but in some of the more routine cases, there would be grounds for the kind of concern shown by the hon. member for Edmonton West. But when we consider that only 12 taxpayers have been sent to jail under this indictment procedure over a six-year period, I think it is very apparent that a good deal of discretion is used before embarking on that sort of prosecution.
It is regrettable, but true, that the fines which are levied by courts against offenders are often viewed simply as a licence fee for lawbreaking-just another cost of doing business- especially if the offender thinks the odds of not getting caught are in his favour. In these circumstances I suggest that the threat of a mandatory jail term, even as short as two months,

November 21, 1980
Income Tax Act
can be a very strong deterrent, especially for the so-called white collar criminal.
There has been widespread public concern, which I share, about the frequency with which offenders under our system of justice are sent to jail or penitentiary. But concern about the proportion of prison terms does not mean that there should be no prison terms. When it appears that fines for tax frauds are not an adequate deterrent, but are instead seen by the offenders as merely a cost of doing business, then I think we have to ensure respect for our laws by a method that will command respect.
I would like to devote some of my remaining remarks to the other proposal in this bill dealing with the present legal requirement for citizens filing an income tax return to identify themselves on the returns by their social insurance numbers. The bill would delete this requirement from the Income Tax Act.
In reading this bill, 1 found it difficult to imagine what might be the motivation behind such a change. Could it represent some sort of latter-day Luddite movement or some sort of emotional revulsion or reaction against one of the tools of a threatening new post-industrial revolution? The social insurance number is, after all, just a tool which, in itself, has no innate evil. In fact it is a tremendously useful tool which, when used reasonably, can provide great social benefits. The requirement is to use it reasonably and responsibly, not to reject it totally.
I think we have to recognize that, in our complex urban society, there exists an emotional reaction among a good many people against what they regard as being depersonalized or reduced to a number in a computer-run society. They feel the system deprives them of some of their humanity. That feeling exists and cannot be ignored. But I suggest we do not resolve the problem by denying to the computers of the Department of National Revenue the use of the SIN.
Unless we drop the use of computers entirely, the Department of National Revenue would simply have to develop letters which would not likely be as good as the highly efficient SIN system. The alternative would be a clumsy, costly, slow system in which the ordinary individuals would find their files confused with the tax returns of others of the same name. I suspect this would be even more frustrating to citizens than being identified by a number.
The usefulness and value of the social insurance number is not always appreciated. We should recognize that income tax returns provide an efficient, low-cost source of essential data for administering the Canada Pension Plan and the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is the social insurance number which is the key link in ensuring that the taxpayer's contributory earnings for Canada Pension Plan purposes are passed on to his or her CPP file. The SIN allows information on insurable earnings to be used for unemployment insurance purposes. If we remove the SIN from income tax returns, I suggest it would simply mean switching to a more cumbersome and costly information system, with separate information returns
having to be filed for Canada Pension Plan and unemployment insurance purposes.
There are other examples of how the SIN on a person's income tax return is useful and valuable, not just to the tax collector but to the taxpayer. Consider, for example, the income-averaging provisions in the Income Tax Act which are designed to compensate for a sudden and irregular upswing in a taxpayer's income in a year. Under the present system, the taxpayer does not have to work out the complicated averaging formula himself on his tax return; he has the assurance that the Department of National Revenue's computer will do that job for him if he qualifies for the income-averaging benefit. But the computer could not do this without the link through the social insurance number which allows the individual's tax return to be correlated with his incomes in preceding years.
When we introduced the child tax credit system only recently, it was clear that the fairest way of measuring a family's financial need was to base it on the aggregate of incomes received by the two parents. Yet this approach would have been extremely difficult without having computer access to the reported incomes of both parents, and the social insurance number made this access possible.
Another example of the number's usefulness is that it makes it possible for National Revenue to cross-check information on incomes and earnings so as to ensure the validity of claims and to detect fraud. We have given National Revenue the responsibility of protecting the integrity of the tax system, and the social insurance number is no more than a reasonable tool which makes this possible.
Our income tax system, after all, is based on self-assessment. I suggest that the average Canadian does not resent paying his fair share of taxes as long as he feels confident that his fellow citizens are doing the same. Does anyone really think such a feeling of confidence would exist if National Revenue did not have the means of cross-checking information on tax returns?
In a democratic society that values individual freedom, we clearly have to strike a balance between the state's need to collect tax revenue and the need for personal privacy. I do not think one can really claim that this balance is seriously upset by requiring us to list our social insurance numbers on our income tax returns.
The use of the social insurance number for income tax administration is only one part of a very much wider issue which has developed quite suddenly in recent years with the advent of the computer era. The basis of the problem was very well described in the report of the Task Force on Privacy and Computers as follows:
One hundred years ago, almost everyone was virtually unknown except in his own village or neighbourhood; today, comprehensive and personal details about everyone are stored in an ever-growing number of files, from education to credit, from welfare to insurance, from taxation to criminal history. By almost every act, from acquiring a passport to buying a car, each citizen leaves a trail of data behind him; the data increases in volume from birth to death and grows ever more comprehensive.
November 21, 1980

I think that is a fair description of the situation, but it does not deal with one of the chief worries of those who are concerned with civil liberties, which is the possibility that these separate bits of information about an individual will somehow be pulled together and pooled without the individual's knowledge or consent. The social insurance number is widely viewed as the villain of the piece-the tool which enables this linkage of personal data from a number of computer-based data banks.
It is true that the social insurance number has been put into use far more widely than was envisaged back in 1964 and I accept some of the concerns of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) who drew attention to that in his remarks.
It now is used as a personal identifier not only in a large number of federal data banks; it is also required by several provincial government acts and programs including the Quebec pension plan and health insurance plan, birth registration in Prince Edward Island, and school registration in Ontario, New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The use of social insurance numbers has also spread outside government and, for example, the Canadian Amateur Hockey Association uses it to keep track of all young hockey players in CAHA leagues across Canada, and the Ottawa Public Library uses it to identify its customers.
I suggest, however, that the real problem is not the existence of the social insurance number. The problem is one of unauthorized data linkage-the pooling of information from different computer data banks. Abolition of the social insurance number would not resolve this problem, because computer technology is such that there are other ways of linking up data. For example, an individual's name, address and birth data could be used to identify his file. That route may be more cumbersome and more costly but it is workable.
I am sure public concern about this issue would be greatly diminished if the public were more widely aware of their present rights on this score, and if they used the defences now available to them in respect of data banks within the federal government.
Part IV of the Human Rights Act, proclaimed on March 1, 1978, attempts to tackle the problem in five ways. I will not read these ways because I know other members want to participate in the debate.
In conclusion, it has been argued that these provisions in the Human Rights Act should be strengthened. However, 1 think they show clearly the direction in which we must move to solve the problem of loss of privacy in the computer age, not only in federal government files but at other government levels and in the private sector as well. I appreciate the concerns of the hon. member for Edmonton West who has brought this topic forward today, but we think an attempt to solve the issue by attacking the social insurance number will be only wasted effort. We would deny ourselves the use of a highly efficient and valuable tool while ignoring the real problem completely.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I say I rise on a question of personal privilege, what I am going to say is not a reflection
Income Tax Act
on the parliamentary secretary, on his personality or anything like that. But it seems to me that there has developed a distressing habit in this House, particularly during the private members' hour when various government speakers are furnished with memoranda written in the departments of the nature read to us this afternoon by the parliamentary secretary which smack of "bureaucratese".
I learned how to speak in this House without notes from a very early date because it was a debating forum. It was not to be an exchange of predetermined memoranda from either source. What I am saying applies as much to hon. members on this side of the House as to the other side. It was not so long ago when the Chair used to intervene when speeches were read. I think reading speeches is a bad habit. Hon. members would not be tolerated on the hustings if they dared appear before their voters with a text in their hands. It is the same thing here. There is a certain tolerance given to hon. members who are starting out, but afterwards one should expect a mastery of the subject and if any hon. member cannot remember enough of the volume put before him, then the speeches will be shorter. I personally do object to having a plethora of read speeches or memoranda in this House whether it is at any stage of legislation or during private members' hour, and as I said, this applies to both sides of the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept the comments made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in good faith. What he has said has a lot to commend it. As he knows, I do not usually speak in this House from complete texts or reports. I have been here a number of years and I usually speak on an impromptu basis. As the hon. member knows, my role with the Privy Council is one which is specialized, and I am not overly knowledgeable about the Income Tax Act.
My colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) tried to be here this afternoon but he had another engagement. He prepared some notes for my help. If I read them at length, I regret that it appeared it was just a pro forma response from bureaucrats to the hon. member. However, let me say to him quite sincerely that the content of his bill was examined by my colleague from Ottawa Centre, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance.
Good points have been raised on this bill and we wish to respond. I take the hon. member's admonition and as one who is concerned with the rules and practices of the House I suggest the comments he has raised could perhaps be more appropriately brought up at another time when we discuss parliamentary reform and we talk about the length of speeches and parliamentary practices. Nevertheless, I welcome his question of privilege although I am not sure it is a question of privilege, but in all honesty I have tried to clarify the situation in response to him.

I do not think the Chair is expected to comment further on the matter of personal privilege that was raised. I might add that my recollection of Beauchesne is that members ought to use notes rather than read speeches. Some of us have difficulty doing that. However, in keeping with the good wishes expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that we have a good weekend, I would state that the hour provided for the consideration of private members' business has now expired. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until two o'clock Monday afternoon.
